one: How much of the stack you rent versus manage yourself, from raw VMs up to finished software.
an: Pizza: make it at home (on-prem), rent a kitchen (IaaS), order delivery and set the table yourself (PaaS), eat at the restaurant (SaaS).
how: IaaS: virtual machines, disks, networks (AWS EC2, DigitalOcean droplets, Hetzner Cloud). You patch the OS, install everything.

PaaS: push code or a container; the platform runs, scales and routes it (Render, Fly, Railway, Cloud Run, AWS ECS Express Mode). Platforms also change direction: see the Production tab for two 2026 examples.
Serverless / FaaS: upload functions; pay per invocation and duration; scale to zero (Lambda, Cloud Run functions, Netlify Functions).
SaaS: finished products you configure (Stripe, Auth0, Sentry). Backend-as-a-Service such as Supabase sits between PaaS and SaaS: a managed Postgres plus auth and storage APIs.
why: Each step up trades control for speed and less ops work. The senior skill is matching the level to the team: a 3-person team running its own Kubernetes is usually a mistake.
trade: Higher levels cost more per unit of compute and lock you into the provider's limits and APIs. Lower levels cost more engineer time.

myth.m: Serverless means there are no servers.
myth.r: There are servers; you just never see or manage them.

q.s: Two developers, one product, modest traffic, no ops experience. Sensible hosting?
o: Self-managed Kubernetes on bare metal
A PaaS (Render/Fly/Cloud Run) with a managed database
Raw VMs with hand-installed everything
Build their own data centre
q.e: Spend scarce engineer time on the product. Move down the stack when a concrete limit forces it.

more: Reserved/committed-use vs on-demand vs spot pricing
Egress costs as a design constraint
lab: Deploy the same small API three ways: a PaaS (Render or Fly), a serverless function (Netlify/Vercel), and a $6 VM with Docker Compose. Record time-to-deploy, monthly cost at idle, and what you had to manage.
Use a provider's pricing calculator to estimate cost at 10 requests/s and 1,000 requests/s for each.

plain:
Cloud services differ in how much they do for you. With IaaS you rent virtual machines and manage everything on them. With PaaS you give them your code or container and they run it. With serverless you give them functions that run only when called. With SaaS you use a finished product.

The more they manage, the less work for you, and the less control and usually higher price per unit.
bridge: Netlify and Vercel are PaaS for frontends. Supabase is closer to SaaS for your backend. A DigitalOcean droplet is IaaS. You have probably already used all three levels.

walk.title: Running the same API at four levels
steps: IaaS (a VM): you install Node, set up systemd, configure nginx and HTTPS, apply security updates. Most control, most work.
Managed containers (Cloud Run, Fly): you give them a Docker image. They run, scale and restart it.
PaaS (Render, Railway): connect the Git repo; it builds and deploys on push.
Serverless functions (Netlify/Vercel functions): you deploy handlers; no server exists while nobody is calling.
For a 2-person team, the higher levels usually win: less ops work means more product work.

terms: Infrastructure as a Service: rented VMs, disks, networks.
Platform as a Service: they run your app for you.
Code runs on demand; you never manage a server.
A finished product you use, like Stripe or Sentry.
Which security and ops tasks are yours vs the provider's.
insights: The level can differ per component. Many teams run the app on a PaaS, Postgres as a managed service, and one heavy job on a plain VM. Mixing levels is normal.
Moving up a level is easy; moving down later is a project. Before going to IaaS “to save money”, price the people and on-call time it adds.

prod.summary: In production the model you choose decides who gets paged at 3 a.m. and what the bill looks like at 10× traffic. Seniors check the shared-responsibility line (who patches, who backs up, who restores), the provider's hard limits, and the exit path if the provider changes direction.
checklist: Write down, per component, who patches the OS, who takes backups and who has tested a restore.
Read the platform's hard limits before committing: request timeout, max memory, payload size, regions offered.
Estimate the bill at today's load and at 10× load; note which line items grow fastest (compute, egress, logs).
Check the vendor's status: is the product still getting features or is it in maintenance mode / closed to new customers?
Keep the app portable where it is cheap to do so: a Dockerfile, plain Postgres, config through environment variables.
Put a billing alert on every account from day one.
numbers: AWS Lambda: max timeout 900 s (15 min), memory 128–10,240 MB, default 1,000 concurrent executions per region.
AWS App Runner: closed to new customers from 30 April 2026; AWS suggests ECS Express Mode instead.
Heroku announced its sustaining engineering model on 6 February 2026: no new features and no new Enterprise contracts.
failures: A nightly report job on serverless fails every night with “Task timed out after 900.00 seconds”.
Lambda's hard limit is 15 minutes. Move long jobs to a container task or a queue of small chunks; do not fight the limit.
The monthly bill on a PaaS triples after a launch, though CPU looks idle.
Usually bandwidth or log ingestion, not compute. Check the bill by line item, put a CDN in front of assets, sample or drop noisy logs.
Data loss after a bad migration on a self-managed VM database; the “backups” cron had been failing for weeks.
On IaaS, backups are your job. Use a managed database or alert when the newest backup is older than 24 h, and test restores.
Your provider announces it will stop selling the product you depend on.
This is why the exit path matters. Containers and Postgres move in days; proprietary queues, auth or functions with custom APIs can take months.

qs.s: A startup runs an API on Lambda. Traffic is now a steady 400 requests/s all day, every day, and the Lambda bill is the largest cost. What is the most reasonable next step?
o: Raise Lambda memory to make each call faster
Compare the cost with the same API on always-on containers (e.g. ECS/Fargate or Cloud Run with min instances), since steady high load is where per-call pricing loses
Move to bare-metal servers in their own rack
Add provisioned concurrency to remove cold starts
qs.e: Per-invocation pricing wins for spiky or low traffic. At constant high load, paying for always-on capacity is usually cheaper. Provisioned concurrency fixes latency, not cost.

qs.s: Your team uses a managed Postgres from a BaaS provider. During an incident review someone asks: “Who is responsible for restoring last Tuesday's deleted rows?” What is the honest answer?
o: The provider; managed means they handle everything
Nobody; deleted data is gone in any cloud
You. The provider keeps the database running and takes backups, but deciding to restore, to which point, and checking the data is your job
The SaaS vendor's support team will do it automatically
qs.e: Shared responsibility: the provider runs the infrastructure and backup mechanism, but your data and the decision and verification of a restore stay with you. Know your plan's point-in-time recovery window.

qs.s: A 3-person team must pick hosting for a new API. Which fact should push them DOWN the stack (towards VMs or managed containers) instead of a PaaS?
o: The team prefers modern tools
They need a background worker that runs for 2 hours, and the PaaS caps requests and jobs at a few minutes
Kubernetes appears in many job ads
The PaaS has a free tier
qs.e: Move down the stack for a concrete limit the higher level cannot meet. A hard job-duration limit is such a limit; fashion and CV value are not.

qs.s: Read this month's bill for an app on a PaaS. Traffic grew 3× after a launch. Which change cuts the most money with the least risk?

Bandwidth (outbound, 4.1 TB)     $410.00

o: Serve static assets and images from a CDN with long cache headers, and stop shipping debug-level and health-check logs
Move the web service to a bigger plan so requests finish faster
Move everything to raw VMs, because compute is cheaper there
Turn off database backups to save money
qs.e: Compute is only $120 of $880. Bandwidth and logs are $670, and both have cheap, safe fixes: a CDN removes most outbound bytes from the origin, and log sampling or level filtering cuts ingestion. Moving to VMs attacks the smallest line and adds ops work.

qs.s: A critical OpenSSL vulnerability is published. Your stack: an API on ECS Fargate (your own Docker image), a worker on an EC2 instance (Amazon Linux), Postgres on RDS, and functions on Lambda using the managed Node.js 22 runtime with default runtime updates. Where must your team act?
o: Nowhere; all four are managed by AWS
Only on RDS, because databases are the most sensitive

Rebuild and redeploy your container images, and patch the EC2 instance; AWS patches the Fargate hosts, the Lambda managed runtime and the RDS engine (you may still need to apply pending RDS maintenance)
Only on Lambda, because functions run untrusted input
qs.e: Shared responsibility moves with the service level. On EC2 the OS is yours. On Fargate AWS patches the host, but the OpenSSL inside your image is part of your image. Lambda managed runtimes are updated by AWS unless you pinned the runtime version or ship a container image.

qs.s: This rate limiter works on a laptop. In production on a serverless platform, users can send far more than 100 requests per minute. Why?

code.title: api/limit.ts

o: Date.now() is not allowed in serverless functions

Each instance has its own memory, instances start and stop all the time, so every instance counts separately and the counts are lost on cold starts; keep the counter in a shared store (Redis, the database) or use the platform's rate limiting
The Map is cleared after every request because functions are stateless by law
The limit should be 1,000, not 100
qs.e: Module-level memory survives between warm invocations of one instance, so the code seems to work in a quick test. But 20 instances means 20 separate counters, and new instances start at zero. State that must be shared belongs outside the function.

qs.s: An API runs on Lambda at a steady 100 requests/s, 24/7. Each call takes 100 ms with 512 MB memory. Using x86 us-east-1 prices ($0.20 per million requests, $0.0000166667 per GB-second) and ignoring the free tier, roughly what is the monthly bill (30 days)?
o: About $27
About $52
About $2,680
About $268
qs.e: Requests: 100 × 2,592,000 s = 259.2 M → 259.2 × $0.20 ≈ $52. Compute: 259.2 M × 0.1 s × 0.5 GB = 12.96 M GB-s × $0.0000166667 ≈ $216. Total ≈ $268. Two small always-on containers often cost much less at this steady load; $52 is only the request charge.

interview.q: We are starting a new product. How would you choose between serverless functions, a PaaS, managed containers and plain VMs?
answer: Start from constraints, not tools: team size and ops skill, traffic shape (spiky vs steady), job durations, compliance (private networking, data residency), budget.
Default to the highest level that meets them: a PaaS or managed containers plus a managed database. Ops time is the scarcest resource in a small team.
Serverless fits spiky or low traffic, webhooks and glue code; it loses on steady high load (per-call pricing), long jobs (Lambda max 15 min) and many DB connections.
VMs are cheapest per unit but you own patching, backups, TLS and on-call; fine for one box with tested restores, painful as the fleet grows.
Keep an exit path: a Dockerfile, plain Postgres, config in environment variables. Write an ADR with a “revisit when” trigger such as a bill threshold.
followups: At what traffic would you move off serverless, and how would you measure it?
What would make you choose VMs over a PaaS on day one?

interview.q: Explain the shared responsibility model. Give an example where teams get it wrong.
answer: The provider secures and runs what it manages (hardware, hypervisor, managed service internals); you own what you configure and put in: data, identities, network rules, your code and images.
The line moves with the level: on EC2 you patch the OS; on Fargate you still own the image contents; on RDS you own users, parameters, restore decisions.
Common mistake: “managed database, so backups are handled” — but nobody tested a restore or knows the point-in-time window.
Another: a public S3 bucket. S3 is secure by default (Block Public Access on); making it public is the customer's configuration.
A good team writes down, per component, who patches, who backs up, and who has rehearsed a restore.
followups: Who is responsible for encrypting data at rest on RDS?
How would you prove your backups work?

interview.q: How do you reduce vendor lock-in without paying too much for it?
answer: Lock-in is a cost to manage, not a sin. Accept it where the managed service saves a lot (e.g. SQS, IAM) and keep the core portable.
Cheap portability: containers, standard Postgres, S3-compatible APIs, OpenTelemetry for observability, config through environment variables, IaC.
Expensive portability (multi-cloud abstraction layers, running the same stack on two clouds) is rarely worth it before a real business reason.
Wrap proprietary APIs behind a small interface in your code so a migration touches one module.
Watch vendor direction: products closed to new customers (AWS App Runner, April 2026) or in maintenance mode (Heroku, February 2026) are signals to plan an exit.
followups: Which managed services would you never try to abstract away?
How long would a move off your current provider take?

t: Platform choice: PaaS vs containers vs Kubernetes
one: The decision tech leads actually make: where should this run, given team size, traffic, budget and skills?
an: Choosing between a taxi, a leased car and running a bus company. All move people; the overhead differs wildly.
how: PaaS / serverless (Render, Railway, Fly, Vercel, Netlify): fastest to ship, least ops; costs climb at high steady load; limits on long-running work and private networking.
Managed containers (ECS on Fargate, ECS Express Mode, Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps): your Docker image, their scheduler. A middle ground most teams can operate.
Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS): maximum flexibility and portability; needs people who understand it, plus upgrades every few months.
VMs (a droplet or Hetzner box with Docker Compose): cheap and simple for one box; you own patching, backups and uptime.
why: This choice dictates hiring, on-call load and monthly cost for years. Interviewers ask "how would you deploy this?" to hear the reasoning, not a product name.
trade: Write down the criteria (cost at expected load, team skills, compliance, lock-in tolerance, time to first deploy) and score options. Revisit when facts change.

myth.r: Plenty of large, profitable products run on PaaS or a few VMs. Fit beats prestige.

q.s: What is the strongest reason to move from a PaaS to Kubernetes?
o: It looks better on a CV
Concrete needs the PaaS cannot meet (cost at scale, networking, compliance), plus people to run it
Kubernetes is free
Faster local development
q.e: Migrate for a measured reason and with the skills in place, not by default.

more: Scoring criteria: cost curve, ops burden, compliance, lock-in, team skills
Hidden costs: bandwidth, logs, managed DB tiers
Multi-tenant vs dedicated hosting for B2B

plain:
Deciding where an app runs is one of the most expensive decisions a tech lead makes, because it determines cost, how much ops work the team does, and what is easy or hard for years.

The goal is a fit between the platform and the team, traffic and budget, not the most impressive technology.
bridge: You already made this choice when you picked Netlify for a frontend. For a full product the same reasoning applies, with more options and more at stake.

walk.title: Writing the decision for a new product
steps: List the facts: 2 developers, expected 20 requests/second, Postgres needed, budget $50/month, no ops experience.
Options: a PaaS (Render/Railway) + managed Postgres; Cloud Run + Cloud SQL; Kubernetes on GKE; a $10 VM with Docker Compose.
Score each on monthly cost, time to first deploy, who handles outages, how hard it is to move away.
PaaS wins: deploys on day one, no on-call for infrastructure, cost fits.
Write the reason and the “revisit when” trigger (e.g. bill over $500/month or a need for private networking) in an ADR.

terms: A platform that runs your app from code or a container.
You bring an image; the provider schedules and scales it.
How hard it is to move to another provider.
A short document recording a decision and why.
insights: The cheapest option on the invoice is often the most expensive in salaries. One engineer-week per month spent on infrastructure costs more than most PaaS bills.
The choice stays reversible if the app is a container, config lives in environment variables and data sits in plain Postgres. Keep it that way and the platform decision becomes much less scary.

prod.summary: The platform decision is a cost, hiring and on-call decision that lasts years. A senior writes it down with the criteria, the expected bill, who is on call, and a clear “revisit when” trigger, and checks the vendor's own future, not only its features.
checklist: Write an ADR with the options, the criteria (cost at expected load, ops time, compliance, lock-in, team skills) and the chosen option.
Price the real bill: compute plus managed DB tier, bandwidth, logs, NAT, load balancer, and paid seats.
Name who is on call for the platform itself (cluster upgrades, node failures) and whether they agreed.
Check hard limits: request timeout, max instance size, private networking, static outbound IPs, regions.
Check the vendor's direction: roadmap, recent deprecations, whether the product is closed to new customers.
Add a “revisit when” trigger, e.g. bill above $X per month or a compliance need the platform cannot meet.
numbers: Kubernetes ships a minor release about every 4 months and each is supported for about 14 months upstream, so a cluster needs at least one upgrade per year.
AWS App Runner closed to new customers on 30 April 2026; existing services keep running but get no new features.
Heroku entered a sustaining engineering model on 6 February 2026: stability and security fixes only.
failures: Six months after moving to Kubernetes, feature work has slowed and one engineer spends most of the week on the cluster.
The team bought operational load without the people for it. Move to managed containers, or budget a real platform role. Decide with numbers, not prestige.
A customer's security review requires that the database is not reachable from the internet, and the PaaS only offers a public endpoint.
A compliance need the platform cannot meet is a valid reason to move. Check private networking and static egress IPs before signing contracts, not after.
The EKS console warns that the cluster version reaches end of standard support next month, with extended support costing extra per hour.
Nobody owned upgrades. Put cluster upgrades on the calendar and in someone's job, or choose a platform that does them for you.
The PaaS bill doubles in one month with flat traffic.
Usually a plan or pricing change, bigger log volume, or a forgotten preview environment. Read invoices by line item each month and tag or delete stale environments.

qs.s: Your product runs on a PaaS for $300/month. A new hire proposes Kubernetes because “we will need it at scale”. Traffic is flat and nobody on the team has run a cluster. What should a tech lead do?
o: Approve it; scale will come
Approve it but run Kubernetes on VMs to save money
Ask which concrete limit the PaaS fails today, record the decision and a revisit trigger, and stay on the PaaS until a trigger is hit
Move to serverless functions instead
qs.e: Platform changes need a measured reason and people to run the result. An ADR with a “revisit when” trigger answers the fear of future scale without paying for it today.

qs.s: Two options for an API at ~50 requests/s steady: a PaaS at $250/month, or a self-managed VM at $40/month that will need about 4 engineer-hours per month of patching and on-call work. Engineers cost about $80/hour. Which is cheaper in total?
o: The PaaS ($250 vs $360)
The VM ($40 vs $250)
They cost exactly the same
Cannot compare money and time
qs.e: VM total = $40 + 4 × $80 = $360 per month, more than the PaaS at $250. Engineer time is the cost people forget to include.

qs.s: You must choose between ECS on Fargate and EKS for 6 stateless services. The team knows Docker but not Kubernetes. Nothing needs Kubernetes-only tools. Which choice fits, and why?
o: ECS on Fargate: same container images, no cluster to upgrade, a smaller skill gap
EKS: it is always more portable, so always better
EKS: Fargate cannot run more than one service
Neither: rewrite everything as Lambda functions
qs.e: Managed containers give most of the benefit with far less to operate. Portability only matters if you will actually move, and you can still move containers later.

## Decision
Use Render (web service + managed Postgres) for the API.

## Consequences
+ Deploy on push, no infra on-call
- Higher cost per CPU than VMs

## Revisit when
We outgrow it.

o: It should have chosen Kubernetes
ADRs should not list negative consequences
The decision should be made by the CTO alone
“We outgrow it” is not measurable; a trigger needs numbers or events, e.g. “bill above $1,500/month”, “p95 above 300 ms at normal load”, or “a customer requires private networking”
qs.e: A revisit trigger exists so that someone notices when the facts change. A vague trigger never fires. Listing downsides is exactly what makes an ADR useful.

qs.s: An export endpoint on Heroku builds a large CSV. Users report failures, and the router logs show this. What is the right fix?

code.title: heroku logs --tail
code.src:
heroku[router]: at=error code=H12 desc="Request timeout" method=GET
  path="/reports/export?year=2025" dyno=web.2 connect=0ms service=30000ms status=503

o: Upgrade to a bigger dyno so the export runs faster
Turn the export into a background job: return 202 with a job ID, build the file in a worker, store it in object storage, and give the user a short-lived download link
Raise the router timeout to 5 minutes in the app settings
Move the app to another region
qs.e: Heroku's router ends a request that has not started responding within 30 seconds, and that limit is not configurable. Long work belongs in a worker. A bigger dyno may help today and fail again when the data grows.

qs.s: Your 3 EKS clusters (dev, staging, prod) all passed the end of standard support because nobody upgraded them. Control-plane pricing is $0.10 per cluster-hour in standard support and $0.60 in extended support. About how much does the control plane cost now per month (730 h), compared with before?
o: From about $219 to about $1,314
From about $73 to about $438
No change; extended support is free
From about $219 to about $438
qs.e: 3 × $0.10 × 730 ≈ $219; 3 × $0.60 × 730 ≈ $1,314. Six times more for doing nothing. This is the hidden cost of Kubernetes that nobody owns: upgrades must be someone's job.

qs.s: An internal admin tool is used by 10 staff, office hours only. An hour of downtime is annoying but harmless. Options: a $12/month VM with Docker Compose, a $60/month PaaS, or EKS. The team has run Compose on VMs before. What is a sound choice?
o: EKS, so it matches the future production platform
The PaaS, because VMs are never acceptable in production
The VM with Compose, with automated OS updates, nightly database backups copied off the box, and one tested restore
Run it on a developer laptop to save $12
qs.e: Fit beats fashion. Low availability needs and existing skills make a single VM reasonable, as long as backups and restores are real. The PaaS is also fine; EKS adds cost and work with no benefit here.

interview.q: You are tech lead of a 4-person team. How would you deploy a new B2B SaaS product, and how do you defend that choice?
answer: Gather the facts first: expected load, team skills, compliance (SOC 2, private networking, data residency), budget, and time to first customer.
Likely answer: a PaaS or managed containers (ECS on Fargate, Cloud Run) plus managed Postgres. Deploy on day one, no cluster on-call.
Price it honestly: compute, DB tier, bandwidth, logs, NAT, load balancer, seats, plus engineer hours.
Check hard limits before signing: request timeout, static egress IPs, private networking, regions, max instance size.
Record it in an ADR with measurable “revisit when” triggers, so the decision can change when the facts do.
followups: A large customer demands a private database endpoint. What changes?
What would the bill look like at 10× customers?

interview.q: When would you move from a PaaS to Kubernetes, and what must be in place first?
answer: Move for a concrete need: cost at high steady scale, networking or compliance the PaaS cannot meet, workloads it cannot run (GPUs, stateful systems, sidecars).
Consider managed containers first; they solve most of these with far less to operate.
Before moving: people who will own the cluster (upgrades about once a year at least, add-ons, node pools), observability, IaC, a CI/CD path, and an on-call rota.
Count the hidden costs: control plane fees, extended support fees if upgrades slip, load balancers, NAT, engineer time.
Migrate one service first, measure, then decide on the rest.
followups: How would you keep cluster upgrades from slipping?
What would make you move back?

interview.q: What hidden costs do teams miss when they compare hosting platforms?
answer: Data transfer: internet egress, cross-AZ traffic ($0.01/GB each direction on AWS), NAT gateway processing ($0.045/GB in us-east-1).
Logs and metrics ingestion, which grow with traffic and debug logging.
Idle resources: public IPv4 addresses ($0.005/hour each on AWS), forgotten preview environments, unattached disks, old snapshots.
Support plans and paid seats per developer.
Engineer time for patching, upgrades and on-call, usually the largest cost of all.
followups: How would you find the top cost drivers in an AWS bill?
How do you stop preview environments from piling up?

one: The handful of service categories every cloud offers under different names. Learn the category, then map names.
an: Every city has a post office, bank and library under different brand names. Know what each does and you can navigate any city.
how: Compute: VMs (EC2, Compute Engine), containers (ECS, Cloud Run), functions (Lambda). Storage: object (S3, GCS), block disks (EBS), file shares (EFS).
Databases: managed SQL (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora), key-value (DynamoDB, Firestore), cache (ElastiCache/Memorystore).
Networking: VPC (private network), load balancers (ALB/NLB), DNS (Route 53), CDN (CloudFront).
Identity: IAM (who can do what). Messaging: SQS (queue), SNS (pub/sub), EventBridge, Kinesis/Pub/Sub (streams). Observability: CloudWatch, Cloud Logging.
why: Architecture diagrams, job descriptions and incident reviews speak in these names. Knowing the category lets you reason about any provider.
trade: Managed services save ops time and lock you in. Portable layers (Postgres, containers, S3-compatible APIs) reduce lock-in where it matters.

myth.r: AWS, GCP and Azure lead, but DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Cloudflare, Supabase and Vercel cover many products more simply and cheaply.

q.s: Where should user-uploaded profile photos live?
o: The app server's local disk
Object storage (S3-style) served via CDN, with the DB storing only the key
Inside Postgres as base64
In Redis
q.e: Local disks vanish with containers and do not scale across servers. Object storage is cheap, durable and CDN-friendly.

Equivalent services across AWS, GCP and Azure

Create an IAM user or SSO login for daily work; never use root again.
Draw your own one-page map: for each category (compute, storage, DB, network, identity, messaging), the AWS name, the GCP name, and a simpler alternative you would actually use.

plain:
Every big cloud (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) offers the same few categories of services under different names: compute, storage, databases, networking, identity, messaging and monitoring.

If you learn the categories, you can understand any architecture diagram, whatever the provider.
bridge: When a job ad says “experience with S3, Lambda, RDS”, translate: file storage, serverless functions, managed SQL database. You probably used equivalents already (Supabase Storage, Netlify Functions, Supabase Postgres).

walk.title: Reading a typical architecture diagram
steps: Users → CloudFront (CDN) → ALB (load balancer).
ALB → ECS containers running your API (compute).
API → RDS Postgres (managed database) and ElastiCache Redis (cache).
Uploads go to S3 (object storage). Background jobs go through SQS (queue) to workers.
Everything sits inside a VPC (private network); IAM decides which piece may access which; logs go to CloudWatch.

terms: Where code runs: VMs, containers, functions.
The provider runs backups, updates and failover for you.
Your private network in the cloud.
insights: When you meet a new service, ask three questions: which category is it, what does it cost per unit (hour, GB, request), and what is its quota per region?
Many AWS bills are dominated by plumbing (NAT gateways, public IPv4 addresses, cross-AZ traffic, logs), not by the compute boxes on the diagram.

prod.summary: In real AWS accounts the risk is less about knowing every service and more about structure: separate accounts per environment, MFA on root, billing alarms, tags, and knowing which service quotas you will hit first. Seniors read an architecture diagram and ask “which box is the single point of failure, and which box sends the biggest bill?”.
checklist: Separate AWS accounts for production and non-production (AWS Organizations), not just separate VPCs.
Root user locked with MFA and never used for daily work; people log in through IAM Identity Center (SSO).
An AWS Budgets alert on every account, set below the amount that would hurt.
Cost-allocation tags (team, service, env) enforced, so a bill can be traced to an owner.
Service quotas checked for the launch: Lambda concurrency, vCPU limits for EC2, Elastic IPs.
Every diagram box has an owner, a backup plan and a known failure mode.
numbers: Lambda default concurrency quota is 1,000 per region; new accounts may start lower and get raised automatically with usage.
A public IPv4 address on AWS costs $0.005 per hour (about $3.60 per month), even when idle.
NAT gateway in us-east-1: $0.045 per hour plus $0.045 per GB processed.
failures: A surprise bill of thousands of dollars from GPU instances in a region you never use.
Leaked access keys used for crypto mining. Delete long-lived keys, use SSO and roles, enable GuardDuty, set budget alerts, and deny unused regions with an SCP.
A launch fails with “Rate Exceeded” / TooManyRequestsException from Lambda at about 1,000 parallel requests.
You hit the account concurrency quota. Request an increase in Service Quotas before the launch, and reserve concurrency for critical functions.
Nobody can say which team owns a $4,000/month line in Cost Explorer.
Resources were created without tags. Enforce tags with IaC and tag policies, and review the top 10 cost items monthly.
A developer deletes a production table while “testing in staging”.
Staging and production shared one account and one set of credentials. Separate accounts make that mistake much harder.

qs.s: A diagram shows: CloudFront → ALB → ECS tasks in two AZs → RDS Postgres (single-AZ) and S3. Which box is the obvious single point of failure?
o: CloudFront
The ALB
S3
RDS Postgres (single-AZ)
qs.e: ALB and ECS span two zones, CloudFront and S3 are regional or global managed services. A single-AZ database goes down with its zone. Multi-AZ fixes that.

qs.s: A job ad lists “SQS, SNS, EventBridge”. A teammate says they are three names for the same thing. What is the best correction?
o: SQS is a queue (one consumer group pulls work), SNS is pub/sub fan-out (push to many subscribers), EventBridge is an event bus that routes events by rules
They are all databases
SQS and SNS are the same; EventBridge is a cron tool only
All three are streaming logs like Kafka
qs.e: Queue, fan-out and rule-based routing solve different problems. Kinesis is the streaming one.

qs.s: Your company has one AWS account for dev, staging and production. What is the strongest reason to split into several accounts?
o: AWS charges less per account
Accounts are a hard boundary for permissions, quotas and blast radius: a mistake or leaked key in dev cannot touch production
It is required to use more than one region
Each account gets a separate free tier forever
qs.e: An account is the strongest isolation unit in AWS. VPCs and tags separate networks and bills, not IAM permissions.

qs.s: Every night at 02:00 a task must call a partner API and save the result. It takes about 3 minutes. Which AWS design fits best?
o: An SQS queue, because queues run jobs on a schedule
An EC2 instance running cron 24/7
An EventBridge Scheduler rule that invokes a Lambda function (with retries and a dead-letter queue)
CloudFront, because it caches the partner response
qs.e: A scheduler plus a function runs only when needed and fits well inside Lambda's 15-minute limit. EC2 with cron works but you pay and patch 24/7. SQS holds messages; it does not create them on a timetable.

qs.s: Finance asks why “EC2-Other” is the largest line. You group Cost Explorer by usage type. What is the most likely cause, and what fixes it?

code.title: Cost Explorer — EC2-Other by usage type
code.src:
Usage type                      Usage          Cost
APN2-EBS:SnapshotUsage          41,200 GB-Mo   $2,060
APN2-EBS:VolumeUsage.gp3         6,000 GB-Mo     $547
APN2-NatGateway-Hours              1,460 Hrs       $86
APN2-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes   2,100 GB       $21

o: Old EBS snapshots that are never deleted; add retention with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup and delete orphaned snapshots
The NAT gateway; add VPC endpoints
gp3 volumes are too expensive; switch to gp2
Cross-AZ traffic; move everything into one AZ
qs.e: Snapshot storage dominates: 41,200 GB-months is far more than the 6,000 GB of live volumes, a sign of years of daily snapshots with no retention. NAT and data transfer are small here; read the numbers before applying a favourite fix.

qs.s: This SCP is attached to the production account's OU. An attacker uses a leaked key of an IAM user with AdministratorAccess in that account and tries to start GPU instances in us-west-2. What happens?

code.title: scp-allowed-regions.json

o: The instances start, because AdministratorAccess overrides SCPs
The request is denied: an SCP limits every principal in a member account, including administrators and the account's root user
The instances start, because SCPs apply only to users created after the SCP
The request is denied only if the user has MFA enabled
qs.e: An SCP sets the maximum permissions for a member account; an explicit Deny there wins over any Allow. Global services (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, STS) are excluded with NotAction because they are served from us-east-1. SCPs do not apply to the management account.

qs.s: When an order is placed, three independent things must happen: send an email, update analytics, reserve stock. Each must retry on its own failures. Which design fits?
o: One SQS queue that the three services all read from
Three cron jobs that poll the orders table every minute
Call the three services synchronously from the checkout request
An SNS topic (or EventBridge rule) that fans out to three SQS queues, one per consumer, each with its own dead-letter queue
qs.e: With one shared queue the consumers compete: each message goes to only one of them. Fan-out gives each consumer its own copy and its own retry and DLQ. Synchronous calls make checkout fail when analytics is down.

interview.q: Draw a typical web application on AWS and explain why each piece is there.
answer: DNS (Route 53) → CDN (CloudFront) for static assets and caching → load balancer (ALB) in public subnets.
Compute in private subnets across at least 2 AZs: ECS/Fargate tasks or EC2 in an Auto Scaling group.
Data: RDS/Aurora Postgres Multi-AZ, ElastiCache for cache/sessions, S3 for files (private, served via CloudFront or presigned URLs).
Async work: SQS queues and workers; SNS/EventBridge for fan-out and events.
Cross-cutting: IAM roles per service, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch logs/metrics/alarms, CloudTrail, budgets.
Then point out the single points of failure and the biggest cost lines.
followups: Where would you put a WAF?
What changes if traffic grows 50×?

interview.q: How would you structure AWS accounts for a startup that is growing from 5 to 50 engineers?
answer: AWS Organizations with separate accounts: management (billing only), security/log archive, shared services, and per-environment workload accounts (dev, staging, prod).
People sign in through IAM Identity Center (SSO) with permission sets; no IAM users with long-lived keys.
SCPs for guardrails: deny unused regions, deny disabling CloudTrail/GuardDuty, deny leaving the organization.
Organization-wide CloudTrail into the log archive account; budgets and cost-allocation tags per account.
Use a landing-zone tool (Control Tower or IaC) so new accounts come with the baseline.
followups: Why accounts instead of VPCs or tags for isolation?
Who should have access to the management account?

interview.q: The AWS bill tripled overnight. How do you investigate?
answer: Cost Explorer grouped by service, then by usage type and region, daily granularity, to find which line jumped and when.
Unexpected region or instance type (GPU) suggests leaked credentials: check CloudTrail for who created what, rotate keys, check GuardDuty findings.
Data-transfer spikes: NAT processing, cross-AZ, internet egress; check VPC Flow Logs and recent deploys.
Request-driven services (Lambda, S3 requests, CloudWatch Logs) often grow from a retry loop or debug logging.
Afterwards: budget alerts with anomaly detection, tags enforced, and a postmortem.
followups: How would you stop it happening again?
What alerts would have caught it within an hour?

one: Cheap, practically unlimited, durable storage for files ("objects") addressed by key, accessed over HTTP.
an: A huge valet parking lot for files: hand it a file and a ticket name, get it back later by name. You do not care which floor it is on.
how: Buckets hold objects; keys look like paths (avatars/u42/2026.jpg) but it is a flat key space.
Objects are written whole (no editing bytes in place). Durability is designed for "11 nines" by storing copies across facilities.
Presigned URLs: the server signs a short-lived URL so the browser uploads or downloads directly, without file bytes passing through your API.
Storage classes trade price for access speed (hot, infrequent, archive); lifecycle rules move or delete old objects.
why: Uploads, exports, backups, static sites, data lakes. The S3 API has become a standard many providers implement (R2, Spaces, MinIO, Supabase Storage).
trade: Public buckets are a classic data-leak headline. Default private, serve through presigned URLs or a CDN with controlled access. Egress (downloading out of the cloud) can cost more than storage.

myth.m: Files must be uploaded through my API so I can check them.
myth.r: Presigned uploads go straight to storage, and you can still control them. A presigned POST policy can enforce size (content-length-range) and type; a presigned PUT can pin the content type but not the size. After the upload, an event triggers a job that checks the real file before you use it.

q.s: Users upload 500MB videos and your API servers run out of memory proxying the bytes. Fix?
o: Bigger servers
Issue presigned upload URLs so the browser uploads directly to object storage
Base64 the video
Use WebSockets
q.e: Your API only signs permission. The heavy bytes skip it entirely.

more: Presigned POST with size and content-type conditions
S3-compatible providers (R2, Spaces, MinIO, Supabase Storage)
lab: Run MinIO in Docker (S3-compatible).
Write an endpoint that returns a presigned PUT URL; upload a file from the browser directly with fetch(url, {method: 'PUT', body: file}).
Generate a presigned GET URL with a 60-second expiry and confirm it stops working after.
docs: AWS: Sharing objects with presigned URLs

plain:
Object storage (Amazon S3 and similar) holds files of any size, in practically unlimited amounts, cheaply and safely. You store a file under a key (like a path) and fetch it by that key over HTTP.

Your app servers should not store user files on their own disks, because those disks disappear with containers and are not shared between servers.
bridge: Supabase Storage and Firebase Storage are object storage with nicer APIs. When you upload a profile picture there and get a URL back, that is this concept.

walk.title: Uploading a large video without overloading your API
steps: The browser asks your API: “I want to upload a 400 MB video of type video/mp4.”

Your API checks that the user may upload, picks the key itself (videos/u42/7f3c…e1.mp4, a random ID, never the user's file name), and creates a presigned URL: a temporary upload link, valid for about 10 minutes, signed with the server's credentials.
The browser uploads the file directly to object storage using that link (in parts, with multipart upload, for big files). The 400 MB never touches your API server.
Storage sends an event (for example an S3 event notification to a queue). A background job checks the real size and type and processes the video.
Your database stores only the key and the file's status, not the file.

terms: A container for objects, with its own settings.
A stored file / its name (looks like a path).
A temporary signed link to upload or download one object.
Data downloaded out of the cloud; often billed.
insights: Treat the key layout as an API. A prefix like tenant/type/id makes lifecycle rules, IAM scoping and “delete everything for this customer” simple.
The database row and the object can drift apart: a row with no file, or a file with no row. Keep an upload status column and run a cleanup job for orphans.

prod.summary: In production, object storage problems are rarely about storing bytes. They are about access: public buckets that leak data, presigned URLs that fail with 403 because of a header mismatch, CORS blocking browser uploads, and egress bills. Seniors check Block Public Access, key naming, lifecycle rules and how uploads are validated after they land.
checklist: S3 Block Public Access stays on; public content goes through a CDN (CloudFront with origin access control), not a public bucket.
Presigned URLs are short-lived (minutes, not days) and created only after the server checks the user may write that key.
Keys include a random or user-scoped part (uploads/u42/uuid.jpg); never trust the client's file name as the key.
Bucket CORS allows only your origins and the methods you use; expose ETag if the browser does multipart uploads.
Lifecycle rules: abort incomplete multipart uploads after a few days; move or expire old objects.
Versioning on buckets that hold data you cannot regenerate, so an overwrite or delete can be undone.
After upload, verify size and real content type in a background job before using the file.
numbers: Amazon S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (“11 nines”) durability.
S3 presigned URLs signed with SigV4 last at most 7 days; if signed with temporary (role) credentials, they stop working when those credentials expire.
S3 multipart upload: parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB, at most 10,000 parts per upload.
Since April 2023, new S3 buckets have Block Public Access on and ACLs disabled by default.
failures: Browser upload with a presigned PUT returns 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch.

The request differs from what was signed: usually a different Content-Type header, or extra headers. Send exactly the headers that were signed: sign the real, allow-listed content type the browser will send. Dropping Content-Type from the signature makes the 403 go away, but then any type can be uploaded (see the code example).
Console shows “has been blocked by CORS policy” when uploading straight to the bucket.
The bucket has no CORS rule for your origin and method. Add a CORS config with your exact origins, PUT/POST, and the headers you send.
The storage bill keeps rising, but the list of objects is small.
Incomplete multipart uploads (or old versions with versioning on) are billed but not listed as normal objects. Add an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule and expire noncurrent versions.
Presigned download links shared in emails stop working after a few hours, though you set 7 days.
The URL was signed with temporary role credentials, so it dies when the session expires. Use short links generated on click instead of long-lived links.
A security scanner finds customer invoices readable by anyone with the URL.
The bucket or objects were made public to “make images work”. Turn Block Public Access back on and serve through a CDN or presigned GETs.

code.title: Presigned upload URL with AWS SDK v3
code.note: signableHeaders is the line that matters: AWS SDK v3 signs only host by default, so without it a URL made for image/png also accepts text/html. With it, a different Content-Type gets 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch. A presigned PUT cannot cap file size; use a presigned POST with a content-length-range condition when size matters.

qs.s: Your presigned PUT URLs sign the Content-Type header (ContentType: "image/png" plus signableHeaders: new Set(["content-type"]) in getSignedUrl). Some users get 403 SignatureDoesNotMatch; all of them upload JPEGs. What is happening?
o: The URL expired
The browser sends Content-Type: image/jpeg, which does not match the signed header
S3 does not accept JPEG files
The bucket is in a different region
qs.e: Signed headers must match exactly. Sign the real content type the client will send (after checking it is allowed). An expired URL gives an “Request has expired” error instead. Note: AWS SDK v3 signs only host by default; without signableHeaders there is no 403 here, but also no protection: the client can upload any Content-Type.

qs.s: You must stop users uploading files larger than 10 MB directly to S3. Which approach actually enforces it at upload time?
o: Check file.size in the browser before upload
A presigned PUT URL with a short expiry
Set a bucket policy that limits object size
A presigned POST with a content-length-range condition of 0–10485760
qs.e: Browser checks can be bypassed and a presigned PUT has no size condition. A presigned POST policy with content-length-range makes S3 itself reject larger uploads.

qs.s: A bucket of 2 TB serves product images, downloaded about 50 TB per month by users worldwide. Finance asks why S3 costs so much. Most likely cause and fix?
o: Storage price; move to Glacier
Too many PUT requests; batch them
Data transfer out (egress) dominates; serve the images through a CDN and cache them for a long time
Versioning; turn it off
qs.e: Storing 2 TB is cheap; moving 50 TB out per month is the expensive part. A CDN with long cache lifetimes cuts egress from the bucket. Glacier would make reads slow and costly.

qs.s: Read this upload endpoint. What is the most serious problem?

code.title: routes/upload.ts

o: expiresIn must be in milliseconds

The key comes from the client, so any user can overwrite another user's file (e.g. send invoice-2026.pdf); generate the key on the server with the user ID and a random ID, and allow-list the content type
Presigned URLs cannot be created inside an Express handler
The route should use GET instead of POST
qs.e: Keys are a flat namespace: the same key means the same object, so a PUT replaces it. A user-chosen key lets one user replace another's files. expiresIn is in seconds, so 3600 is one hour (long, but not the main bug).

qs.s: Browser uploads from https://app.example.com to a presigned PUT URL fail. The console says the request “has been blocked by CORS policy”. Here is the bucket CORS config. What must change?

code.title: bucket-cors.json

o: Set AllowedOrigins to ["*"]
Turn off Block Public Access
Add PUT to AllowedMethods and allow the headers the browser sends (at least Content-Type) in AllowedHeaders
Make the presigned URL expire later
qs.e: The preflight asks for method PUT and header Content-Type; neither is allowed, so the browser blocks the request. CORS has nothing to do with public access, and a wildcard origin is not needed: your own origin is already listed.

qs.s: A telemetry service writes every event as its own S3 object: 400 million PUTs per month, about 1 KB each. S3 Standard in us-east-1 charges $0.005 per 1,000 PUT requests. What does that cost per month, and what is the fix?
o: About $2,000 in PUT requests alone, while storage costs only about $9; batch events into larger files (for example one file per minute, or a Firehose stream)
About $20; nothing to fix
About $200,000; move to Glacier
Nothing; PUT requests are free
qs.e: 400,000,000 / 1,000 × $0.005 = $2,000. The data is only about 400 GB (around $9 at $0.023/GB). With many tiny objects the request price, not the storage price, dominates.

qs.s: A developer adds await sleep(2000) after every upload “because S3 is eventually consistent, so a read right after a write can return the old file”. What do you say in review?
o: Good idea; 2 seconds is the documented delay
Increase it to 10 seconds to be safe
Use a different region for reads
Remove it: since December 2020 S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs, overwrites, deletes and LIST, so the next read after a successful write returns the new data
qs.e: The eventual-consistency advice is outdated. Sleeping hides real bugs (such as reading before the upload actually finished) and adds latency. Caches in front of S3, such as a CDN, can still serve old copies; that is a cache problem, not an S3 one.

interview.q: Design file uploads for a web app where users upload videos of up to 2 GB.
answer: Do not proxy the bytes through the API: issue presigned URLs, using multipart upload for large files (parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts).
The server authorizes the user, picks the key (user prefix + random ID), allow-lists the type, and keeps expiry short.
Enforce size with a presigned POST policy, or validate after upload and delete files that are too big.
An S3 event to a queue triggers processing (virus scan, transcode); the DB stores key and status (pending → ready).
Lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads; serve downloads via CloudFront or short-lived presigned GETs.
Configure CORS for your origins, PUT, and exposed ETag (needed to complete multipart uploads from the browser).
followups: How do you resume an upload after the network drops?
How do you stop someone uploading 2 TB on your bill?

interview.q: How do you make sure a bucket never leaks customer data?
answer: Keep Block Public Access on at account and bucket level; it is on by default for new buckets since April 2023.
No public ACLs (ACLs disabled, bucket owner enforced); access through IAM roles, bucket policies and presigned URLs.
Public content goes through CloudFront with origin access control, so the bucket itself stays private.
Encrypt (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS); with KMS, key policies add a second lock.
Detect: IAM Access Analyzer for external access, AWS Config rules, Macie for sensitive data, CloudTrail data events for audit.
followups: How would you share one file with a partner for a week?
What does SSE-KMS protect against that SSE-S3 does not?

interview.q: Object storage costs keep growing. Where do you look?
answer: Split the bill: storage by class, requests (PUT/GET), data transfer out, and retrieval fees.
Hidden storage: noncurrent versions with versioning on, incomplete multipart uploads; fix with lifecycle rules.
Cold data: lifecycle transitions to Infrequent Access or Glacier classes, or Intelligent-Tiering when access is unknown; watch minimum storage durations and retrieval fees.
Egress: put a CDN in front of popular objects with long cache lifetimes.
Many tiny objects: batch them, because request charges dominate.
followups: When is Glacier a bad idea?
How would you find which prefixes use the most space?

one: Code that runs on demand per request or event, scales automatically, and costs nothing when idle.
an: Hiring a taxi per trip instead of owning a car. No parking fees, but each ride has a pickup delay, and daily commuting adds up.
how: You deploy a handler; the platform spins up instances as requests arrive. Billing per invocation and duration.
Cold start: a new instance must load your code first (tens of ms to seconds). Warm instances are reused.
Triggered by HTTP, queues, file uploads, schedules, DB changes. Edge functions are lighter variants running in CDN locations with limited runtime APIs.
why: Ideal for spiky or low traffic, glue code, webhooks and scheduled tasks. You do not manage servers or scaling.
trade: Execution time limits, cold starts, connection storms against databases (see connection pooling), and costs that exceed a small server at high steady load. Local development and debugging are harder.

myth.r: At low or spiky traffic, yes. At high constant traffic, an always-on container is usually cheaper.

q.s: A function calls Postgres and works in testing, but fails under a traffic spike with 'too many connections'. Why?
o: Cold starts
Each concurrent instance opens its own DB connection
CORS
TLS expiry
q.e: Scaling out to hundreds of instances means hundreds of connections. Use a pooler or an HTTP-based DB driver.

more: Cold start factors: bundle size, runtime, VPC attachment
lab: Deploy a function to Netlify or Vercel that returns the time. Measure the first request after 10 minutes idle vs the next one.
Add a big dependency and measure the cold start again.
Make the function connect to Postgres and run a load test with 100 concurrent requests; watch the connection count in Postgres (select count(*) from pg_stat_activity).

plain:
With serverless functions you write a function, deploy it, and the platform runs it when a request or event arrives. You pay per call. With no traffic, nothing runs and you pay nothing.

When a function has not run for a while, the first call must start a fresh instance first. That delay is called a cold start.
bridge: Netlify Functions and Vercel API routes are serverless functions. If your API is sometimes slow on the first request after a quiet period, that is a cold start.

walk.title: A spike of traffic on serverless
steps: Normal day: 2 requests/second, each taking about 200 ms. Concurrency (instances busy at once) = requests per second × duration = 2 × 0.2 ≈ 1 instance.

A post goes viral: 300 requests/second. Now 300 × 0.2 = 60 instances must run at the same time. If a slow database makes each request take 1 s, it becomes 300 instances. The platform starts them in seconds. You did nothing.
New instances have cold starts: the first request on each takes an extra 300 ms to 1 s.
Each instance opens its own database connection. Postgres reaches max_connections and starts refusing (“too many clients already”). Fix: a connection pooler and a concurrency cap.
The spike ends; idle instances are shut down; the bill shows exactly what was used.

terms: One deployed handler, run on demand.
Delay when a new instance must start before handling a request.
How many instances run at the same time.
A lighter function running in CDN locations.
insights: Do the concurrency maths before a launch: requests per second × seconds per request = instances. Compare the result with your concurrency quota and your database's connection limit.
A slow dependency raises cost and concurrency at the same time, because you pay for the time a function spends waiting, and waiting functions hold instances.

prod.summary: In production, serverless trouble comes from its limits, not its code: cold starts on user-facing paths, concurrency quotas, timeouts, and databases flooded by connections. Seniors set timeouts and concurrency on purpose, keep bundles small, reuse clients across invocations, and watch throttles and duration percentiles.
checklist: Create DB and HTTP clients outside the handler, so warm invocations reuse them.
Use a connection pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, Supavisor) or an HTTP-based driver; cap the pool at 1–2 per instance.
Set the function timeout below the caller's timeout (e.g. API Gateway's), and set reserved concurrency so one function cannot starve others.
Make event handlers idempotent: queues and async invocations deliver at least once and retry.
Add a dead-letter queue or on-failure destination for async and queue triggers.
Bundle and tree-shake (esbuild); measure the INIT duration in logs after each dependency change.
Alert on Throttles > 0, error rate, and p99 duration close to the timeout.
numbers: AWS Lambda: timeout up to 900 s; memory 128–10,240 MB; at 1,769 MB a function gets the equivalent of one vCPU.
AWS Lambda default concurrency: 1,000 per region; each function can add up to 1,000 execution environments every 10 seconds.
AWS Lambda synchronous payload: 6 MB request and 6 MB response; zip package 50 MB zipped, 250 MB unzipped.
Since 1 August 2025, AWS bills the Lambda INIT (cold start) phase for all functions, including zip functions on managed runtimes.
failures: Postgres logs FATAL: sorry, too many clients already during a traffic spike.
Each concurrent instance opened its own connections. Put a pooler in front, set pool size 1 per instance, and cap function concurrency below what the DB can take.
CloudWatch shows Throttles rising and clients get 429 TooManyRequestsException.
Account or reserved concurrency is exhausted. Request a quota increase, or move bursty work behind a queue that the function drains at a fixed rate.
Logs say Task timed out after 3.00 seconds on a function that calls a slow API.
3 s is Lambda's default timeout. Set an explicit timeout per function, and add your own shorter timeout on outbound calls so you can fail cleanly.
A queue-triggered function processes the same order twice and charges a customer twice.
At-least-once delivery plus a retry after a timeout. Use an idempotency key (order ID) stored with a unique constraint before doing the side effect.
p99 latency is 2 s while p50 is 80 ms, mostly after quiet periods.
Cold starts. Shrink the bundle, avoid heavy init work, or use provisioned concurrency / SnapStart for latency-critical paths.

code.title: Lambda handler that reuses one DB connection
code.note: The pool lives outside the handler, and max is 1 because a Lambda environment serves one request at a time. 500 concurrent instances still mean up to 500 connections, which is why the URL points at a pooler.

qs.s: A Lambda function has reserved concurrency 50. Each call takes 200 ms. Roughly how many requests per second can it handle before throttling?
qs.e: Each environment handles one request at a time: 1 / 0.2 s = 5 requests/s per environment, × 50 = 250 requests/s. Above that you get throttles.

qs.s: A webhook handler on Lambda must call a payment provider that sometimes takes 40 s. API Gateway's integration timeout is 29 s by default. What is the right design?
o: Raise the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
Retry the payment call 3 times inside the handler
Increase Lambda memory so the call is faster
Accept the webhook quickly (store it, return 200), and process it asynchronously from a queue with its own timeout and retries
qs.e: The caller gives up at 29 s whatever the Lambda timeout is. Separate “receive” from “process” with a queue; that also gives retries and a dead-letter queue.

qs.s: Reading this code inside a Lambda handler: export const handler = async () => { const client = new Pool({ max: 10 }); ... }. What is the main production problem?
o: A new pool, and new connections, is created on every invocation and never reused, so connections pile up during spikes
Pools are not allowed in Lambda
max should be 100
async handlers cannot use Postgres
qs.e: Clients belong outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them. Inside, every call pays the connection cost and can leak connections; with max 10 per instance, a spike multiplies the damage.

qs.s: Analytics events from this Lambda handler arrive late, out of order, or not at all. Why?

code.title: handler.ts

o: When the handler returns, Lambda freezes the execution environment, so the unawaited request may pause mid-flight and resume (or time out) only when the next invocation thaws it; await it, or put the event on a queue
Lambda blocks all outbound HTTP calls
JSON.stringify is asynchronous in Lambda
The analytics service rate-limits Lambda IP addresses
qs.e: After the response, Lambda freezes the process; background promises do not keep running. Work that must finish must be awaited before returning, or handed to a durable queue.

qs.s: Read this Lambda log line. Which conclusion is correct?

code.title: CloudWatch Logs
code.src:
REPORT RequestId: 3f1c... Duration: 812.45 ms Billed Duration: 1213 ms
  Memory Size: 1024 MB Max Memory Used: 1019 MB Init Duration: 400.12 ms

o: Billed Duration is wrong and should be reported to AWS
The function is cold-start bound only; memory is fine

Memory use is at 99.5% of the limit, so a slightly larger input may kill the environment (“Runtime exited with error: signal: killed”); raise memory or find what grows (often a module-level cache). Billed time includes the 400 ms INIT phase
Init Duration means the function timed out
qs.e: 812 ms + 400 ms init ≈ 1213 ms billed: since August 2025 AWS bills the INIT phase. The real risk is memory: 1019 of 1024 MB. Memory that grows across warm invocations is usually a cache or array at module level.

qs.s: An SQS-triggered function receives batches of 10 messages. When 1 message fails, all 10 are processed again, and customers get duplicate emails. What is the right fix?

code.title: worker.ts

o: Set the batch size to 100 so failures are rarer
Catch all errors and ignore them
Delete the queue's dead-letter queue

Enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and return { batchItemFailures: [{ itemIdentifier: messageId }] } for only the failed messages; also make sending idempotent (record sent message IDs)
qs.e: If the handler throws, the whole batch becomes visible again and is retried. Partial batch responses retry only the failed items. Idempotency is still needed, because SQS delivers at least once.

qs.s: Function A handles 2,000 requests/s at 300 ms per call. Function B, in the same account and region, uses about 500 concurrent executions at peak. The account concurrency quota is the default 1,000. What happens at peak?
o: Nothing; 2,000 requests/s is below the 10,000 limit
Throttling: A alone needs 2,000 × 0.3 = 600 concurrent executions, plus 500 for B = 1,100 > 1,000; request a quota increase and reserve concurrency for the critical function
Only cold starts get slower; nothing is rejected
A gets all 1,000 and B gets 0, because A is busier
qs.e: Concurrency = rate × duration. The quota is shared by all functions in the region, so one busy function can starve another; reserved concurrency guarantees (and caps) a share for one function.

interview.q: When would you NOT use serverless functions?
answer: Steady high load: per-invocation pricing usually loses to always-on containers.
Long or heavy jobs: Lambda has a 15-minute maximum, limited memory/CPU, and no GPUs; use containers or batch jobs.
Latency-critical paths that cannot tolerate cold starts, unless you pay for provisioned concurrency or SnapStart.
Workloads with long-lived connections or in-memory state (WebSockets servers, caches); state must live elsewhere.
Heavy relational DB use without a pooler, because concurrency multiplies connections.

interview.q: How do you connect Lambda functions to Postgres safely under load?
answer: Create the client outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it; pool size 1 per environment.
Put a pooler in between: RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, Supavisor; or use an HTTP-based driver (Neon, Data API).
Cap function concurrency (reserved concurrency) below what the database can take.
Set short connect and query timeouts, shorter than the function timeout, so failures are clean.
Watch the DB: connection count, too many clients already errors, and pooler wait time.
followups: What does RDS Proxy do with idle connections?
Why can transaction-mode pooling break prepared statements?

interview.q: A queue-triggered function sometimes processes messages twice and sometimes gets stuck on one bad message. How do you fix both?
answer: Duplicates are normal with at-least-once delivery and retries after timeouts; make the handler idempotent (idempotency key with a unique constraint before the side effect).
Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least 6 × the function timeout (AWS guidance for Lambda), so in-flight messages are not redelivered.
Use partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures) so one failure does not retry the whole batch.
Add a dead-letter queue with a maxReceiveCount so a poison message moves aside after a few attempts.
Alert on DLQ depth and on the age of the oldest message.
followups: How would you replay messages from the DLQ?

sequenceDiagram

  participant P as Platform
  participant F as New instances
  participant DB as Postgres

  Note over P: 300 × 0.2 s = 60 busy instances

diagrams.caption: What to notice: the platform scales in seconds without help, but every new instance is a new database client. The database, not the function, decides whether the spike survives.

one: Running code in CDN locations close to users, not in one central region.
an: Instead of every customer phoning headquarters, small branch offices answer simple questions locally.
how: Edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Netlify Edge Functions on Deno, Vercel's Edge runtime) use lightweight V8 isolates: almost no cold start, but only Web APIs plus a subset of Node, no file system, and small memory (Cloudflare: 128 MB per isolate).
One isolate can serve many requests at the same time, so module-level variables are shared between users. Keep per-request data inside the handler.
Good for: redirects, auth checks on a signed cookie, A/B bucketing, geolocation, rewriting HTML, personalising cached pages.
Bad for: anything that talks a lot to a central database, because each query still crosses the world to reach it.

The trend in 2026 is back towards regional Node: Vercel recommends migrating from its Edge runtime to Node.js, and Next.js 16.3 deprecates runtime = 'edge' for routes and pages (Node.js is the default).
why: Shaves latency for logic that does not need central data. Use it for small, data-free decisions; keep data-heavy logic next to the database.
trade: Moving compute to the edge while the DB stays in one region can make things slower: several cross-ocean round trips instead of one. Data location dictates where compute should be.

myth.r: Only when the work is local. Edge function + 5 queries to a DB in Virginia is slower than running next to the DB.

q.s: An edge function makes 4 sequential queries to a database in us-east-1 for a user in Seoul. Better design?
o: Add more edge locations
Run that logic in a region near the database (or replicate the data near users)
Use HTTP/3
Lower DNS TTL
q.e: Latency is dominated by the round trips to the DB. Put compute next to the data.

docs: Cloudflare Learning: What is edge computing?

plain:
Edge computing runs your code in CDN locations near users instead of in one central region. It is great for small decisions that need no central data: redirects, checking a cookie, choosing a language, A/B test buckets.

It is bad for code that talks to a central database many times, because each query still travels to wherever the database is.
bridge: Cloudflare Workers and Netlify Edge Functions run at the edge. Next.js middleware was edge-only for years, which is why some Node APIs were missing there; in Next.js 16 it is renamed proxy.ts and runs on the Node.js runtime by default.

walk.title: When edge makes it faster, and when slower
steps: Assume one round trip between Seoul and a US region takes about 150 ms.
Faster: a user in Seoul hits an edge function in Seoul that reads their language cookie and redirects to /ko. Total: about 20 ms.
The same logic in a US region would cost at least one 150 ms round trip.
Slower: an edge function in Seoul runs 4 queries, one after another, against a database in the US: 4 × 150 ms = 600 ms.
A regular function next to the database: 4 × about 5 ms, plus one 150 ms round trip to the user ≈ 170 ms. Rule: put compute next to the data it needs most.

terms: Servers in many locations close to users.
A lightweight sandbox (V8) used by edge runtimes.
One geographic location where your main servers and data live.
insights: Count round trips, not kilometres. The edge wins when a request needs zero or one trip to the origin.
Treat edge code like a CDN rule with logic: small, stateless, and with caching headers set on purpose, so one user's answer is never served to another.

prod.summary: At the edge, production problems come from where the data lives and from runtime limits: a Node library that will not load, a CPU-time limit, or many round trips to a database on another continent. Seniors keep edge code small and data-free, measure end-to-end latency from real user locations, and pin data-heavy routes to the database's region.
checklist: List every network call the edge code makes; if it needs the main database more than once, run it regionally instead.
Check each dependency works without Node built-ins (fs, net, native modules) before choosing the edge.
Know the CPU, memory and bundle limits of your platform and measure CPU time per request.
Make edge logic safe to fail open or closed on purpose (e.g. auth check fails closed).
Pass decisions downstream in headers or cookies; do not try to share in-memory state between isolates.
Measure p50/p95 latency from 3–4 real regions, not just from your laptop.
numbers: Cloudflare Workers: 10 ms CPU time per request on the Free plan; on Paid the default is 30 s and it can be raised to 5 minutes. Time spent waiting on network calls is not CPU time. 128 MB memory per isolate.
Cloudflare returns error 1102 “Worker exceeded resource limits” when a Worker goes over its CPU or memory limit.
Vercel Edge runtime: must begin sending a response within 25 s; code size limit after gzip is 1 MB (Hobby), 2 MB (Pro), 4 MB (Enterprise).
Next.js 16: proxy.ts defaults to the Node.js runtime, and setting the runtime option in proxy throws an error.
failures: Deploy fails or the function crashes with “The edge runtime does not support Node.js 'crypto' module” / Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'.
A dependency needs Node built-ins. Use a Web-API-based library (Web Crypto, jose for JWT) or run that route on the Node runtime.
Cloudflare returns error 1102 “Worker exceeded resource limits”.
The Worker went over its CPU-time or memory limit, often from parsing a large JSON or rendering heavy HTML. Move the heavy work to a regional service or cache the result.
Pages got slower after moving SSR to the edge; traces show 4 sequential DB calls of 150 ms each.
Compute moved away from the data. Pin the route to the DB's region, batch queries, or add a read replica near users.
Users in one country keep getting the wrong language, even after changing it.
The edge redirect is cached by the CDN for everyone in that location. Add Vary on the cookie or mark the redirect Cache-Control: private, no-store.

code.title: Cloudflare Worker: country redirect without touching a database
code.note: Everything it needs is in the request (cookie, country), so it finishes in a few ms near the user. The private, no-store header stops a shared cache from sending one user's redirect to everyone.

qs.s: A user in Seoul. Option A: edge function in Seoul making 3 sequential queries to a DB in Virginia (~180 ms round trip each). Option B: one request from Seoul to a server in Virginia (~180 ms) that makes the 3 queries locally (~2 ms each). Roughly which is faster?
o: A: about 540 ms vs B: about 186 ms, so B wins
A wins because edge is always closer
They are the same
A: about 186 ms vs B: about 540 ms
qs.e: In A every query crosses the Pacific: 3 × 180 ms. In B only the user's request crosses once, and the queries are local. Put compute next to the data it talks to most.

qs.s: You move JWT verification into Next.js 16 proxy.ts and add export const config = { runtime: 'edge' } to keep it “fast”. What happens?
o: It runs at the edge as before
Next.js throws an error: the runtime option is not available in proxy, which runs on Node.js
It silently falls back to the browser
JWT verification stops working only in development
qs.e: In Next.js 16 proxy defaults to the Node.js runtime and setting runtime there throws. The old edge-only middleware model is gone.

qs.s: Which job is the best fit for an edge function?
o: Generating a monthly PDF report from 50,000 database rows
A checkout that writes to 4 tables in a transaction
Resizing uploaded 4K videos
Checking a signed session cookie and redirecting unauthenticated users to /login before the cached page is served
qs.e: Cookie checks need no central data and finish in milliseconds, so serving them near the user is pure win. The others are data-heavy, long-running or CPU-heavy.

qs.s: Read this Cloudflare Worker. Under load, some users see another user's account page. Why?

code.title: worker.ts

o: Workers cache responses by default
verifySession must be synchronous
One isolate handles many requests at the same time; currentUser is module-level, so a second request can overwrite it while the first awaits the API. Keep per-request data in local variables
Response.json is not supported at the edge
qs.e: Module-level state is shared by every request in the isolate. During the await, another request runs and replaces currentUser. The same bug exists in any Node server; edge just makes it easy to forget. (The code also ignores the profile response status.)

qs.s: An edge function adds “Hello, Dilnoza” to the HTML of the home page. After deploy, users see other people's names. Here are the response headers. What is wrong?

code.title: response headers
code.src:
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
cache-control: public, max-age=300
vary: Accept-Encoding

o: The personalised HTML is marked public, so the CDN caches one user's page and serves it to everyone for 5 minutes; cache only the shared shell and personalise after the cache (or mark the personalised response private, no-store)
HTTP/2 does not support cookies
max-age should be 3600
The content-type header is missing a charset
qs.e: Personal data and shared caches do not mix. The good pattern is a cached shared page plus a small edge step that adds the personal part to each response without storing it in the shared cache.

qs.s: A Worker on Cloudflare's Free plan (10 ms CPU per request) calls an origin API that takes 800 ms to answer, then returns the JSON unchanged. Will it hit the CPU limit?
o: Yes; 800 ms is far above 10 ms
No; waiting for a network response is not CPU time. It would hit the limit if it did heavy work itself, such as parsing and transforming a multi-megabyte JSON
Yes, unless the origin is also on Cloudflare
No, because Free plan Workers have no limits
qs.e: Edge CPU limits measure time the isolate spends computing, not wall-clock time. I/O-bound proxies fit well; CPU-heavy parsing, image work or rendering is what triggers error 1102.

qs.s: A store has users worldwide and one Postgres database in Frankfurt. The product catalog is read 1,000× more often than it changes; orders are writes. Which design gives low latency with the least complexity?
o: Move Postgres to an active-active multi-region cluster
Run all API code at the edge, querying Frankfurt directly
Put the database in the region with the most users and accept slow pages elsewhere
Cache catalog responses at the edge/CDN (short TTL plus stale-while-revalidate, purged on change) and keep order writes in a regional API next to the database
qs.e: Read-heavy, rarely changing data is perfect for edge caching. Writes need the database, so they stay next to it. Active-active databases solve this too, but at a huge cost in complexity.

interview.q: When does moving logic to the edge make an app faster, and when slower?
answer: Faster when the logic needs only data that is in the request or in an edge cache: redirects, signed-cookie checks, A/B buckets, geo rules, cache-key tweaks.
Slower when it needs the central database several times: every query crosses the distance between edge and region (e.g. 4 × 150 ms).
Rule: place compute next to the data it talks to most; count round trips, not distance to the user.
Runtime limits matter too: no Node built-ins or native modules, small memory, CPU limits.
Measure p50/p95 from several real regions before and after.
followups: How would you serve personalised pages fast worldwide?
What does a regional read replica change?

interview.q: How would you personalise a heavily cached page without breaking caching?
answer: Cache the shared shell publicly at the CDN; keep personal data out of it.
Add the personal parts at the edge per request (HTML rewriting) or in the client from a small private API call.
If a response varies by cookie or header, either mark it private/no-store or include that value in the cache key; never cache personal HTML as public.
Keep the number of variants small (language, country, A/B bucket), otherwise the hit rate collapses.
Test with two different users through the real CDN, not only locally.
followups: What is the risk of Vary: Cookie?
How do you purge cached pages after a price change?

interview.q: Compare V8 isolate runtimes with container-based serverless.
answer: Isolates start in milliseconds and many run in one process, so cold starts are tiny and cost is low; containers or microVMs take longer to start but run any language and binary.
Isolates offer Web APIs and a subset of Node; no file system, native modules or raw TCP in general (some platforms add sockets).
Limits are tight: memory (128 MB on Workers), CPU time per request, bundle size.
Isolates share a process, so module-level state is shared between concurrent requests.
Choose isolates for small, latency-sensitive request logic; containers for heavy, long or library-rich work.

Where would you keep state for an edge app?
