one: A region is a geographic area (Seoul, Frankfurt). Inside it, availability zones are separate data centres with independent power and networking.
an: Spreading your savings across several banks in one city (zones) protects against one bank failing; keeping some in another country (regions) protects against the whole city flooding.
how: Running replicas across 2–3 zones in one region survives a data centre failure with little latency cost (zones are a few ms apart).
Multi-region protects against a whole region outage but brings real cost: data replication across continents, consistency questions, more complex failover.
Data residency laws may require data to stay in a country.
why: Interviewers ask "what happens if a data centre goes down?". Multi-AZ is the standard answer for production; multi-region is a business decision with a price.
trade: Multi-region active-active is one of the hardest things in infrastructure. Most companies run multi-AZ with backups restorable in another region.

myth.r: Whole regions have had multi-hour outages. Design for zone failure at minimum.

A managed multi-AZ setup with automatic failover, plus tested backups
A bigger instance
A CDN
q.e: Multi-AZ covers the common failure (one facility) at modest cost.

docs: AWS: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

plain:
A region is a geographic location of a cloud, like Seoul or Frankfurt. Inside a region there are several availability zones: separate data centres with their own power and network. In AWS they are many kilometres apart, but all within about 100 km of each other, so latency between them is low.

Running copies in two or three zones protects you if one data centre fails. Running in several regions protects you if a whole region fails, but is much more complex.
bridge: When you create a Supabase or Neon project and pick a region, you choose where your data lives. Choosing one far from your users adds latency to every query.

walk.title: What happens when one data centre loses power
steps: Your app runs 2 instances in zone A and 2 in zone B; your managed database (RDS Multi-AZ) has its primary in A and a synchronous standby in B.
Zone A loses power.
The load balancer's health checks fail for zone A instances, so traffic goes only to zone B within seconds to a minute (depending on the check interval and threshold).
RDS promotes the standby in zone B and points the database DNS name at it. AWS says this typically takes 60–120 seconds.
Apps must reconnect (and must not cache the old DNS answer for long). Users see a 1–2 minute blip, then the app works. With everything in one zone, it would have been down until the zone recovered.

terms: A geographic area with several data centres.
One isolated data centre within a region.
Running copies across zones in one region.
Running in several regions; protects against regional outages.
Laws requiring data to stay in a country.
insights: Zone failures are rarely clean. A zone often gets slow or partly broken instead of fully down, so health checks should test real dependencies, not only “the process is up”.
Multi-region without a rehearsed failover is only a second bill. Practise the switch on a schedule, and measure the real RTO you achieved.

prod.summary: In production, “multi-AZ” is the baseline and the details decide whether it works: are instances really spread across zones, do clients reconnect after a DB failover, and is there spare capacity in the surviving zones? Multi-region is a business decision measured with RTO (how long you may be down) and RPO (how much data you may lose).
checklist: App instances spread across at least 2 AZs, with enough headroom that the remaining zones carry full load if one fails.
Database in a Multi-AZ setup; failover tested by a forced reboot-with-failover in staging.
Clients reconnect on errors and respect short DNS TTLs (JVM: networkaddress.cache.ttl of 60 s or less).
Backups copied to a second region, and a restore there rehearsed at least once.
App and database in the same region; cross-region calls only where designed.
Written RTO/RPO targets agreed with the business before paying for multi-region.
Data residency requirements checked for each region you store personal data in.
numbers: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ (single standby) failover typically takes 60–120 seconds.
AWS keeps the AZs of a region within about 100 km of each other, giving single-digit-millisecond latency between them.

AWS charges $0.01/GB in each direction for EC2, RDS, ElastiCache and network-interface traffic between AZs in the same region, so 1 GB from AZ a to AZ b costs $0.02 in total. Replication between an RDS primary and its Multi-AZ standby is not charged.

On Linux, a TCP connection to a host that vanished without closing it can hang for about 15 minutes before the kernel gives up (default tcp_retries2 = 15), unless the app sets its own timeouts or keepalive.
failures: After a planned RDS failover, some app instances throw timeouts for about 15 minutes, then recover on their own.

The pool kept sockets to the old primary, and with no socket timeout or TCP keepalive the kernel waits for retransmissions to time out. Set connect/query timeouts, enable keepalive, validate connections on borrow, and respect a short DNS TTL. (Java caches DNS for 30 s by default, but forever if a security manager is installed or networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1.)
One AZ goes down and the site still falls over, although “we are multi-AZ”.
All replicas were scheduled in one zone, or the other zone had no spare capacity. Use topology spread constraints / AZ-balanced groups and size for N-1 zones.
Every page takes 300 ms longer after moving the app to a cheaper region.
The database stayed in the old region, so each query crosses regions. Keep the app and DB in the same region.
The DR plan fails during a drill: snapshots in the second region cannot be restored.
The encryption key existed only in the first region, or the copy job had been failing silently. Use multi-region keys or re-encrypt on copy, and alert on copy job failures.

code.title: AZ names differ per account; AZ IDs do not
code.src:
# us-east-1a in your account may be a different data centre than us-east-1a in a partner's account.
# Compare by Zone ID when you need to be in the same (or a different) physical AZ.
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId]' --output table

# Force a Multi-AZ failover in staging to see how your app behaves
aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier staging-db --force-failover
code.note: AWS maps zone names like us-east-1a to physical zones differently for each account; the ZoneId (e.g. use1-az1) is the same everywhere. A forced failover is the cheapest real test of your reconnect logic.

qs.s: Your app runs 4 instances at 70% CPU each, 2 per AZ in 2 AZs. One AZ fails. What happens to the survivors, and what should you change?
o: Nothing changes, 70% stays 70%
Load drops because users leave
The 2 survivors must carry 4 instances' load, about 140% CPU, so they overload. Run with enough headroom (or 3 AZs) to survive losing one zone
The load balancer queues requests until the zone recovers
qs.e: Multi-AZ only helps if the remaining zones can carry the full load. Plan capacity for N-1 zones.

qs.s: The business says: “We can be down for 4 hours and lose up to 15 minutes of data in a regional disaster.” Which design matches this most cheaply?
o: Active-active in two regions with synchronous writes
Single region, Multi-AZ database, plus continuous backups or a cross-region replica in a second region, and a rehearsed restore runbook
Single AZ with daily snapshots in the same region
A bigger database instance
qs.e: An RTO of 4 h and RPO of 15 min fits warm standby or backup-and-restore with frequent log shipping. Active-active is far more expensive than needed; same-region daily snapshots miss both targets.

qs.s: A partner says “our service is in us-east-1a, put yours there too for low latency.” You do, but latency is not better. Why?
o: us-east-1a is overloaded
Latency does not depend on zones
Their DNS is slow
AZ names are mapped per account, so your us-east-1a may be a different physical zone; you should compare Zone IDs
qs.e: AWS shuffles zone names per account to spread load. The Zone ID (like use1-az4) identifies the same physical zone across accounts.

qs.s: This Deployment runs 6 replicas on a cluster with nodes in 3 AZs. Looking at where the pods landed, what is the risk, and what fixes it?

code.title: kubectl get pods -o wide (zone added)
code.src:

api-7d9f8c-2kq4x      1/1    ip-10-0-1-21     ap-northeast-2a
api-7d9f8c-8hv2m      1/1    ip-10-0-1-21     ap-northeast-2a
api-7d9f8c-c5wzn      1/1    ip-10-0-1-37     ap-northeast-2a
api-7d9f8c-k9p1d      1/1    ip-10-0-1-37     ap-northeast-2a

api-7d9f8c-z8m3q      1/1    ip-10-0-1-21     ap-northeast-2a

o: No risk; Kubernetes moves pods automatically within a second
Losing zone 2a takes out 5 of 6 replicas; add topologySpreadConstraints on topology.kubernetes.io/zone with maxSkew: 1, and keep spare capacity in every zone
The pods need more CPU requests
Use a bigger node in zone 2a
qs.e: The scheduler does not spread pods evenly across zones unless you ask. Rescheduling after a zone failure takes time and needs free capacity in the other zones, which may not exist. Spread constraints plus N-1 capacity make multi-AZ real.

qs.s: Service A runs in AZ a and sends 50 TB per month to service B in AZ b (same region). AWS charges $0.01/GB in each direction between AZs. Roughly what does this traffic cost per month?
o: About $500
Nothing; traffic inside a region is free
About $1,000
About $5,000
qs.e: 50,000 GB × ($0.01 out + $0.01 in) = $1,000 per month. Fixes: keep chatty pairs in the same zone where safe (zone-aware routing), compress, or cut the volume. $500 counts only one direction.

qs.s: A business owner says: “Our RPO for a full region outage must be zero.” The database is in Seoul, and the DR region is Tokyo with about 30 ms round trip. What is the honest trade-off?
o: Asynchronous cross-region replication already gives RPO zero
RPO zero is impossible in any cloud
Daily snapshots copied to Tokyo give RPO zero

RPO zero needs every commit confirmed in both regions (synchronous replication), adding at least about 30 ms to every write and making writes fail when the link is down; most teams accept a few seconds of RPO with async replication instead
qs.e: Async replicas lag, so the last seconds of writes can be lost: that lag is your RPO. Synchronous cross-region commits remove the loss but put the round trip on every write. Snapshots give an RPO of hours.

qs.s: Read the Terraform for a production database. Which statement about its availability is true?

code.title: rds.tf
code.src:
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  identifier              = "prod-main"
  engine                  = "postgres"
  instance_class          = "db.r7g.large"
  multi_az                = false
  backup_retention_period = 7
  availability_zone       = "ap-northeast-2a"
}

o: If zone 2a fails, the database is down until the zone recovers or you restore from backup into another zone (with data loss back to the last restorable time)
Backups make it highly available: RDS fails over to a backup automatically
db.r7g instances are automatically replicated to 3 AZs
It survives a zone failure because the region has 4 AZs
qs.e: Backups protect data, not uptime. Without multi_az = true there is no standby to promote. A point-in-time restore takes time and can lose the last few minutes of writes.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens to your system when one availability zone fails.
answer: Load balancer health checks fail for targets in that zone and traffic shifts to healthy zones within seconds to a minute.
Remaining instances must carry the full load: that only works if you planned N-1 capacity or autoscaling can add capacity in the other zones (and quotas allow it).
The Multi-AZ database promotes its standby (RDS typically 60–120 s); DNS changes; clients must reconnect, with timeouts and keepalive so they do not hang on dead sockets.
Zonal resources fail with the zone: single-AZ caches, EBS volumes, one NAT gateway in that AZ.
Afterwards check the zone-aware pieces: did pods spread, did queues drain, was anything lost?
followups: How would you test this without a real outage?
Which components in your stack are zonal?

interview.q: How do you choose a disaster recovery strategy for a full region outage?
answer: Start with the business: RTO (how long we may be down) and RPO (how much data we may lose), and what that downtime costs.
Backup and restore (hours of RTO, cheap) → pilot light (core data replicated, compute off) → warm standby (scaled-down copy running) → multi-site active-active (seconds, very expensive and complex).
Data is the hard part: async replication gives an RPO of seconds; synchronous adds the inter-region round trip to every write.
Everything the restore needs must exist in the second region: images, keys (KMS), secrets, IaC, DNS plan.
Rehearse it: a DR plan that was never run does not exist.
followups: How would you fail back?
What is the weakest link in your current DR plan?

interview.q: Explain RTO and RPO, and how they drive cost.
answer: RTO: the maximum acceptable time to restore service. RPO: the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.
Lower numbers need more always-running duplicate infrastructure and more complex replication, so cost rises steeply near zero.
Examples: daily snapshots → RPO up to 24 h; continuous backup with point-in-time recovery → minutes; async replica → seconds; sync replica → zero, with write latency cost.
Targets differ per system: payments may need minutes, analytics can wait a day.
Write the targets down with the business and test that you meet them.
followups: What RPO does RDS point-in-time recovery give you?
Who should own these numbers?

one: Your own isolated network inside the cloud, split into public and private subnets with firewall rules.
an: A gated office campus. The lobby (public subnet) faces the street; the server room (private subnet) has no street door at all.
how: Public subnets have a route to the internet (load balancers live here). Private subnets do not (app servers, databases).
Private machines reach out (to download packages, call APIs) via a NAT gateway; nothing can reach in.
Security groups are per-resource firewall rules: "the DB accepts port 5432 only from the app servers' group".
Engineers reach private resources via a bastion host, VPN, or a session manager, not a public DB port.
why: A database with a public IP and a weak password is found by scanners within hours. Network isolation is a core layer of defence.
trade: NAT gateways and cross-zone traffic cost money. Misconfigured routes are a common cause of "it cannot reach the internet" mysteries.

myth.m: The DB has a strong password, so exposing it publicly is fine.
myth.r: Defence in depth: pre-auth vulnerabilities exist. Do not give attackers a door to knock on.

q.s: Where should the production Postgres live?
o: Public subnet with a strong password
Private subnet, security group allowing only the app tier
On a developer laptop
In the CDN
q.e: Only the app needs to talk to it, so only the app can.

more: Route tables, internet gateways, NAT gateways
Bastion hosts vs SSM Session Manager vs Tailscale
lab: Read your cloud provider's default VPC: list its subnets, route tables and security groups.
On DigitalOcean or Hetzner, create two droplets in a private network, put Postgres on one with no public port, and connect from the other.
Use nmap -p 5432 <public-ip> against your own DB host to confirm the port is closed to the internet.

plain:
A VPC is your own private network inside the cloud. Some parts face the internet (public subnet, e.g. the load balancer). Other parts have no internet entrance at all (private subnet, e.g. app servers and the database).

Firewall rules (security groups) say exactly who may talk to whom, for example “the database accepts connections only from the app servers”.
bridge: On Netlify you never see this because there is no server to protect. Once you run your own API and database, this is what keeps the database from being reachable by anyone on the internet.

walk.title: A typical secure layout
steps: Public subnet: only the load balancer, open on port 443 to the world.
Private subnet: app servers. They accept traffic only from the load balancer's security group.
Private subnet: the database. It accepts port 5432 only from the app servers' security group.
App servers call external APIs through a NAT gateway (outbound only; nothing can come in that way), and reach S3 through a free gateway endpoint instead of the NAT.
Engineers reach the database through SSM Session Manager port forwarding or a VPN, with access tied to their identity and logged. No public SSH or database port.

terms: Virtual Private Cloud: your isolated network.
A section of the network, public or private.
A firewall attached to a resource.
Lets private machines reach out to the internet, not the other way.
A hardened entry machine for admins.
insights: Security groups are stateful: reply traffic is allowed automatically. Network ACLs are stateless: they need rules for both directions, including the return ports.
A subnet is “public” only because its route table has a route to an internet gateway. When debugging reachability, read the route tables, not the subnet names.

prod.summary: In production the VPC questions are: what can reach the database, how do private resources get out, and what does that cost? Seniors review security group rules (sources by group, not 0.0.0.0/0), use VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to avoid NAT charges, size CIDRs for growth, and give engineers access through SSM or a VPN instead of open SSH.
checklist: No security group allows 0.0.0.0/0 on database, cache or SSH ports; only the load balancer is open on 443.
Database rules reference the app's security group, not IP addresses.
Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, so that traffic skips the NAT gateway.
NAT that survives a zone failure: one zonal NAT gateway per AZ with per-AZ route tables, or a regional NAT gateway (available since November 2025), which spans the AZs where you have workloads.
CIDR ranges planned so they do not overlap with other VPCs, offices or VPNs you may peer with later, and subnets large enough for growth (EKS gives every pod a VPC IP by default).
Engineer access through SSM Session Manager, a VPN or Tailscale; no public port 22.
VPC Flow Logs on for production, at least for rejected traffic.
numbers: AWS NAT gateway in us-east-1: $0.045 per hour (about $32 per month) plus $0.045 per GB processed.
AWS public IPv4 addresses cost $0.005 per hour each since February 2024, idle or in use.
AWS reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet (the first four and the last), so a /28 (16 addresses, the smallest allowed) leaves 11 usable and a /24 leaves 251.
Data between AZs in the same region costs $0.01/GB in each direction.
failures: The NAT gateway line on the bill is larger than the EC2 line.
Large traffic to S3, ECR or other AWS services goes through NAT at $0.045/GB. Add gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB and interface endpoints for heavy services like ECR.
A Lambda attached to the VPC times out on every call to an external API.
Private subnets have no route to the internet. Add a NAT gateway route for those subnets, or do not attach the function to the VPC if it does not need private resources.
App logs: connect ETIMEDOUT 10.0.12.34:5432 after a new service is deployed.
Timeouts (not “connection refused”) usually mean a security group or NACL drops the packets. Add the new service's security group as a source on the DB's group.
Peering two VPCs fails because both use 10.0.0.0/16.
Overlapping CIDRs cannot be routed. Plan non-overlapping ranges per environment and account from the start; fixing it later means rebuilding the VPC.

code.title: Database accepts Postgres only from the app's security group
code.note: The rule names a group, not IPs, so new app instances get access automatically. Security groups are stateful: reply traffic is allowed without an extra rule.

qs.s: Your private app servers download 3 TB per month from S3 through a NAT gateway in us-east-1. Roughly how much of the NAT bill is data processing, and what removes it?
o: About $135; add a gateway VPC endpoint for S3
About $3; nothing to do
About $1,350; move the servers to a public subnet
Nothing; AWS-to-AWS traffic is always free
qs.e: 3,000 GB × $0.045 ≈ $135 per month on top of the hourly charge. A gateway endpoint for S3 routes that traffic privately and has no per-GB charge.

qs.s: A new service gets connect ETIMEDOUT to Postgres, while the old service connects fine. Both are in the same private subnet. What do you check first?
o: The Postgres password
The DB security group: it allows the old service's group but not the new one's
The NAT gateway
The DNS TTL
qs.e: Same subnet means routing is the same. A timeout (packets dropped) with only one service affected points to security group membership. A wrong password would give an authentication error, not a timeout.

qs.s: You must give 3 engineers occasional psql access to a private RDS database. Which option is the safest with little setup?
o: Give the DB a public IP and allow the engineers' home IPs
Open port 22 on a bastion to 0.0.0.0/0 with key auth
Port forwarding through SSM Session Manager (or a VPN like Tailscale) to a host in the VPC, with access controlled by IAM and logged
Copy the database to their laptops
qs.e: No inbound port is opened, access is tied to IAM identities and sessions are logged. Home IPs change and public DB endpoints get scanned within hours.

qs.s: An EC2 instance without a public IP sits in this subnet. It cannot download packages. Why?

code.title: route table rtb-0a1 (associated with subnet-app-a)
code.src:
Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       igw-0f3c9e2d

o: The local route blocks internet traffic
The security group must allow inbound 443 for downloads
An internet gateway only works for instances with a public IP; this private instance needs 0.0.0.0/0 pointing at a NAT gateway (or a public IP, which you should not give it)
DNS resolution is disabled in all VPCs by default
qs.e: An internet gateway translates between a public IP and a private IP; without a public IP there is nothing to translate. Security groups are stateful, so replies to outbound requests need no inbound rule.

qs.s: The database is in a private subnet with no public IP. Its security group is below. A teammate says “it's private, so 0.0.0.0/0 is fine”. What is the accurate reply?

code.title: db_sg.tf
code.src:
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "db_in" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.db.id
  cidr_ipv4         = "0.0.0.0/0"
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port         = 5432
  to_port           = 5432
}

o: Correct; private subnets make security groups irrelevant

It is not reachable from the internet today, but anything inside the VPC, peered VPCs or the VPN can connect, and one change (a public IP, “publicly accessible”) exposes it; reference the app's security group instead
The database is already exposed to the internet
Security groups cannot use CIDR rules
qs.e: Defence in depth: routing and security groups are separate layers. Here routing is the only protection left. A compromised container anywhere in the network can reach the database port.

qs.s: An EKS cluster uses the default VPC CNI, which gives every pod an IP from the subnet. Nodes are in two /24 subnets. After scaling to 30 nodes running about 30 pods each, new pods stay Pending with “failed to assign an IP address to container”. What is going on?
o: The subnets are out of IPs: two /24s give 2 × 251 = 502 usable addresses, but about 900 pods plus nodes need more; add larger subnets or a secondary CIDR, or use prefix delegation
The nodes are out of CPU
Kubernetes allows at most 110 pods per cluster
The NAT gateway limits the number of pods
qs.e: Each subnet loses 5 reserved addresses (256 − 5 = 251). Pod IPs come from the VPC, so subnet size limits pod count. Plan CIDRs for pods, not only for nodes.

qs.s: Someone added a custom network ACL to the app subnet. HTTPS from the load balancer reaches the servers, but clients get timeouts. What is missing?

code.title: network ACL acl-07b (app subnet)
code.src:
Inbound                          Outbound
100  TCP 443  10.0.0.0/16 ALLOW  100  TCP 443  0.0.0.0/0 ALLOW
*    ALL      0.0.0.0/0  DENY   *    ALL      0.0.0.0/0 DENY

o: Inbound port 80
A security group rule for outbound 443
Nothing; the ACL is correct and the problem is DNS
Network ACLs are stateless, so return traffic needs its own rule: allow outbound TCP to the ephemeral ports (1024–65535) of the load balancer's subnets
qs.e: Replies leave the server from port 443 to the client's random high port. A stateless ACL checks that packet against the outbound rules, which only allow destination port 443. Security groups are stateful and would not need this.

interview.q: Design the network for a typical three-tier web application on AWS.
answer: One VPC per environment with a non-overlapping CIDR (e.g. /16), subnets in at least 2–3 AZs.
Public subnets: load balancer (and zonal NAT gateways if you use them). Private subnets: app tier. Isolated private subnets: databases and caches.
Security groups chained by reference: ALB → app on the app port, app → DB on 5432; nothing else.
Outbound: NAT (one per AZ, or a regional NAT gateway) for the internet; gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB; interface endpoints for heavy AWS APIs like ECR.
Access for humans via SSM Session Manager or VPN; Flow Logs on; IaC for all of it.
followups: How would you connect this VPC to an office network?
How big would you make the subnets, and why?

interview.q: How do private resources reach the internet and AWS services, and what does each option cost?
answer: NAT gateway: outbound only; about $0.045/hour plus $0.045/GB processed in us-east-1; one per AZ (or a regional NAT gateway) for availability.
Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB): route-table entries, no hourly or per-GB charge, so big S3 traffic should never go through NAT.
Interface endpoints (PrivateLink): private IPs for other AWS APIs, hourly per AZ plus per-GB, often cheaper than NAT for heavy ECR or CloudWatch traffic.
Public IPv4 on instances: $0.005/hour each and exposes the instance; avoid for private tiers.
Check the bill: NAT-Gateway-Bytes larger than compute is a common surprise.
followups: How would you find which service sends most NAT traffic?
What changes with IPv6 and an egress-only internet gateway?

interview.q: Security groups versus network ACLs: when do you use each?
answer: Security groups: attached to network interfaces, stateful (replies allowed automatically), allow rules only, can reference other security groups.
Network ACLs: attached to subnets, stateless (you must allow return traffic on ephemeral ports), allow and deny rules, evaluated in number order.
Use security groups as the main control; they express “who may talk to whom” by role.
Use NACLs rarely: subnet-wide guardrails or blocking a specific bad IP range quickly.
Debug drops with VPC Flow Logs (ACCEPT/REJECT) and Reachability Analyzer.
followups: Why do timeouts, not “connection refused”, point at a firewall?
How would you block one attacking IP range fast?

one: Describing servers, networks, DNS and databases in code files, reviewed in PRs and applied by a tool, instead of clicking in a console.
an: An architect's blueprint versus building by memory. You can rebuild the house exactly, review changes before construction, and see who moved a wall.
how: Terraform/OpenTofu (HCL), Pulumi (real languages), CloudFormation/CDK (AWS). You declare resources; the tool computes a plan (diff between code and reality), then applies it.
A state file records what the tool created. Store it remotely with locking, never in git (it can contain secrets).
Modules package reusable pieces ("a standard Postgres with backups and alerts").
why: Reproducible environments, code review for infra changes, disaster recovery (recreate everything), and an audit trail.
trade: Manual console changes cause drift. Learning curve and state management are real. Start by codifying the critical things (DNS, DB, networking).

myth.m: IaC is only for big companies.
myth.r: Even one production DB and DNS zone benefit: the day you need to rebuild, the code is your documentation.

q.s: terraform plan shows it will destroy and recreate the production database. What do you do?
o: Apply, it knows best
Stop. Find which attribute forces replacement, and change approach (or use lifecycle prevent_destroy)
Delete the state file
Run it twice
q.e: Some attribute changes force replacement. Reading the plan is the whole point of the plan step.

more: Remote state backends and state locking
lab: Install OpenTofu or Terraform. Use the Cloudflare or DigitalOcean provider to manage one DNS record as code.
Change the record in the dashboard manually, then run plan and see the drift.
Add a lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to it and try to destroy.

plain:
Infrastructure as Code means describing your servers, databases, DNS records and networks in code files instead of clicking in a web console. A tool (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi) reads the files, compares them with what really exists, and makes the changes.

Infrastructure changes then go through pull requests and review, just like app code.
bridge: It is like moving from editing production by hand to having a repository and CI. Clicking in a console is the infrastructure version of editing files directly on the server.

walk.title: Adding a DNS record with Terraform
steps: You add a few lines describing the record atlas CNAME xq-stack-atlas.netlify.app to a .tf file.
terraform plan shows exactly what will change: “+ create 1 record”. Nothing happens yet.
A teammate reviews the plan in the PR.
terraform apply creates the record. The state file now remembers it exists.
Months later, someone edits the record in the dashboard. The next plan shows the difference (drift), and you decide whether to keep or revert it.

terms: Popular IaC tools using HCL files.
The tool's record of what it created.
Real infrastructure differing from the code.
A reusable bundle of infrastructure code.
insights: Split state by blast radius: network, data and app in separate states, so a bad apply on the app cannot touch the database.
A plan is a snapshot. Save it (terraform plan -out=tfplan) and apply that file, so you get exactly what was reviewed; Terraform refuses a saved plan if the state changed since.

prod.summary: In production, IaC is about safe change: remote state with locking, a reviewed plan for every apply, protection on resources that hold data, and drift detection. Seniors read plans for “forces replacement”, keep secrets out of state where possible, and make CI the only thing that applies to production.
checklist: Remote state with locking (S3 backend with use_lockfile = true, Terraform Cloud, or a GCS backend); never local or in git.
State bucket encrypted, versioned, and readable only by CI and a few admins (state can contain secrets).
Every PR shows the plan output; apply only in CI from the reviewed plan.
prevent_destroy or deletion protection on databases, buckets with data and DNS zones.
Provider and module versions pinned; .terraform.lock.hcl committed.
Use moved blocks when renaming resources, and import blocks to adopt existing ones.
A scheduled plan -detailed-exitcode in CI to detect drift (exit code 2 means changes).
numbers: Terraform's S3 backend supports native locking with use_lockfile (Terraform 1.10+); DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated.
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode returns 0 for no changes, 1 for error, 2 for changes present.
Terraform moved to the Business Source License in August 2023; OpenTofu is the MPL-licensed fork under the Linux Foundation.
failures: Error acquiring the state lock with a lock ID from a CI job that crashed an hour ago.
A run died while holding the lock. Confirm no apply is running, then terraform force-unlock <ID>. Never delete the lock blindly while a run is active.
The plan shows -/+ destroy and then create replacement on the production DB with # forces replacement next to one attribute.
That attribute cannot change in place (e.g. engine, identifier, subnet group). Revert the change, or plan a migration; prevent_destroy would have stopped the apply.
After renaming a resource in code, the plan wants to destroy the old one and create a new one.
Terraform tracks resources by address. Add a moved { from = ... to = ... } block so the state is updated instead.
Two engineers applied from laptops and the state now disagrees with reality.
Local applies and no lock discipline. Make CI the only applier for production and give humans read-only credentials there.
A database password shows up in plain text in the state file.
Terraform stores resource attributes in state. Let the service manage the secret (e.g. RDS manage_master_user_password), encrypt and restrict state, or use ephemeral values where supported.

code.title: Remote state with locking, and a protected database
code.note: Two layers of protection: prevent_destroy stops Terraform, deletion_protection stops anyone through the API. The moved block turns a rename into a no-op instead of a destroy.

qs.s: A scheduled CI job runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode against production every night. Last night it exited with code 2. What does that mean?
o: The plan failed with an error
Real infrastructure differs from the code (drift or unapplied changes); someone should look at the plan
Everything matches
The state lock is held
qs.e: Exit code 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = changes present. A nightly 2 is your drift alarm.

qs.s: You split one big Terraform file into a module and move aws_s3_bucket.uploads into module.storage. The plan wants to destroy and recreate the bucket (with 2 TB of user files). What is the right fix?
o: Apply and re-upload the files
Delete the state file and import everything again
Add a moved block from aws_s3_bucket.uploads to module.storage.aws_s3_bucket.uploads
Rename the bucket so there is no conflict
qs.e: The resource address changed, not the resource. A moved block (or terraform state mv) tells Terraform it is the same object.

qs.s: Your team wants to stop “who applied what” confusion. Which setup gives the strongest guarantee?
o: A rule in the wiki saying “always run plan first”
Committing the state file to git so changes are visible
Giving every engineer admin credentials to apply quickly
Only CI can apply to production, using the plan reviewed in the PR; humans get read-only production credentials
qs.e: A process enforced by permissions beats a rule people can forget. Committing state to git leaks secrets and gives no locking.

qs.s: The nightly drift check shows this plan for production. Nobody changed the Terraform code this week. What should happen next?

code.title: terraform plan (excerpt)

o: Apply immediately; the code is always right
Delete the security group and recreate it
Find who added the rule and why (CloudTrail), then either remove it on purpose or add it to the code; do not let a routine apply silently change it
Ignore it; in-place changes are always harmless
qs.e: Someone opened Redis to one IP in the console. Applying blindly might break a real dependency; ignoring it leaves an unknown hole open. Drift is a question to answer, not a diff to auto-fix.

qs.s: You remove "logs" from this list. The plan wants to destroy and recreate two buckets that still hold data. Why, and what is the fix?

code.title: buckets.tf

o: count tracks resources by index; removing item 0 shifts “uploads” and “exports” to new indexes, so their bucket names change and they must be replaced. Use for_each = toset(var.buckets) (with moved blocks from the old indexes)
S3 buckets cannot be managed in Terraform
The list must be sorted alphabetically
Run terraform refresh and the plan will be fine
qs.e: With count, this[1] was uploads and becomes exports. Because bucket forces replacement, Terraform plans destroy/create. for_each keys resources by name, so removing one item affects only that item.

qs.s: Two CI jobs (plans for two different PRs) run at the same time against the production state. One fails with “Error acquiring the state lock”. What is the right response?

code.title: CI log
code.src:
Acquiring state lock. This may take a few moments...
Error: Error acquiring the state lock
Lock Info:
  ID:        8c1e2f7a-...
  Path:      acme-tf-state/prod/app.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypePlan
  Who:       runner@ci-4821
  Created:   2026-10-02 09:14:03 UTC

o: Add -lock=false to every CI command
Run terraform force-unlock automatically before each job
Delete the lock file from S3 whenever a job fails
The lock worked as designed; serialise jobs per state (CI concurrency group) or use -lock-timeout=5m so the second job waits
qs.e: The lock is held by a live plan on another runner. Disabling or force-removing it invites two writers to corrupt state. Force-unlock is only for a lock left behind by a run that is definitely dead.

qs.s: The app repo's Terraform and the platform repo's Terraform both declare rules for the same security group. Each apply removes the other's rules, and alerts fire after every deploy. What is the real fix?
o: Run the two applies in a fixed order
Add ignore_changes = all to both
Give each resource exactly one owner: one state manages it; the other repo reads it with a data source or outputs (or manages only separate rule resources it fully owns)
Merge the two state files by hand
qs.e: Two states managing the same object always fight, because each thinks the other's changes are drift. Ownership boundaries between states are a design decision; ignore_changes just hides the problem.

interview.q: How do you structure Terraform for several environments and teams?
answer: Split state by environment and by blast radius (network, data, apps), so one apply cannot touch everything and plans stay fast.
Shared, versioned modules for common pieces (a standard Postgres, a service); environments are thin root modules that call them with different inputs.
Remote state with locking (S3 with use_lockfile on Terraform 1.10+, or HCP Terraform); production applied only by CI.
Pin provider and module versions; commit .terraform.lock.hcl.
Pass data between states through outputs or data sources, with one owner per resource.
Workspaces are fine for identical copies; separate directories or stacks are clearer when environments differ.
followups: How would you promote a module change from staging to production?
When would you choose Pulumi or CDK instead?

interview.q: How do you roll out a risky infrastructure change safely?
answer: Read the plan for forces replacement and destroy counts; protect stateful resources with prevent_destroy and deletion protection.
Apply to staging first with the same code and a similar data shape.
Use moved and import blocks for refactors so state changes are reviewed in the PR.
Prefer create-before-destroy and blue/green for replaceable resources; make small changes, one concern per PR.
Have a rollback plan (previous version, snapshot) and apply during a watched window with dashboards open.
followups: What would you do if an apply failed half-way?
How do you test modules?

interview.q: How do you handle secrets with infrastructure as code?
answer: Never commit secrets in .tf or .tfvars files; inject them from a secrets manager or CI secrets.
Remember that state stores resource attributes, including passwords: encrypt the state bucket, restrict access, enable versioning.
Let services generate and own secrets where possible (RDS manage_master_user_password stores it in Secrets Manager).
Use ephemeral values and write-only arguments where the Terraform version and provider support them, so values never reach state.
Rotate secrets on a schedule and after people leave.
followups: Who should be able to read the state file?
How would you rotate a database password managed by Terraform?

diagrams.title: Plan, review, apply, and drift
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD
  CODE[".tf files in a PR"] --> PLAN["terraform plan"]
  STATE[("Remote state + lock")] --> PLAN
  REAL["Real infrastructure"] -->|"read current"| PLAN
  PLAN --> DIFF["Diff: + create 1 record"]
  DIFF --> REV{"Teammate approves?"}
  REV -->|no| CODE
  REV -->|yes| APPLY["terraform apply in CI"]
  APPLY --> REAL
  APPLY -->|"record what exists"| STATE
  CLICK["Edit in dashboard"] -.->|drift| REAL
diagrams.caption: What to notice: plan compares three things (code, state, reality). A manual dashboard edit changes reality behind the code, and the next plan shows it as drift.

Fix: required_version raised to >= 1.11, where use_lockfile became GA. Practice: the count-vs-for_each plan was reproduced for real with terraform_data (2 replaced, 1 destroyed; for_each + moved destroys only “logs”).

videos.why: Infrastructure as Code as a concept, before any specific tool.

one: The cloud's permission system: which person or service may perform which action on which resource.
an: Hotel key cards. Each card opens specific doors for a specific period. Housekeeping's card does not open the safe.
how: Principals (users, roles, service accounts) get policies: allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::avatars/*.
Services should assume roles with short-lived credentials, not use long-lived access keys pasted into env vars.
CI systems can use OIDC federation: GitHub Actions proves its identity to AWS and gets temporary credentials, with no stored keys at all.
why: Leaked long-lived keys with admin rights are behind many cloud breaches and surprise crypto-mining bills.
trade: Tight policies are tedious to write; broad ones (*:*) are a breach waiting to happen. Start narrow and widen with evidence.

myth.m: Our app needs admin access to work.
myth.r: It needs a handful of specific actions on specific resources. Find them and grant only those.

q.s: A CI pipeline uses an AWS access key with AdministratorAccess stored as a repo secret. Best improvement?
o: Rotate it yearly
Use OIDC to assume a narrowly scoped role with temporary credentials
Put it in the code
Email it to the team
q.e: No static secret to leak, and the blast radius is limited to what deployment actually needs.

more: Roles and trust policies (who may assume a role)
Access Analyzer to find unused permissions
Workload identity in Kubernetes (IRSA, GKE Workload Identity)
lab: Write an IAM policy that allows only s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on one bucket prefix. Test it with the policy simulator.
Set up GitHub Actions OIDC to assume a role and list that bucket with no stored keys.
docs: GitHub: Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services

plain:
IAM decides who (a person or a program) may do what action on which resource in your cloud account. For example: “the upload service may write files into the avatars bucket, and nothing else”.

Programs should get short-lived permissions through roles, not long-lived secret keys stored in config.
bridge: It is the cloud version of route guards and roles in your app, but for infrastructure: which service can read which bucket, which pipeline can deploy, which developer can delete a database.

walk.title: Deploying from GitHub Actions without stored keys
steps: Old way: an AWS access key with admin rights is pasted into GitHub secrets. If it leaks, the attacker owns your account.
New way: in AWS, create a role “deploy-api” that may only update one service and push to one registry.
Allow that role to be used only by your specific GitHub repo's workflow (OIDC trust).
During the workflow, GitHub proves its identity to AWS and receives temporary credentials valid for one hour.
No long-lived key exists anywhere to leak, and even the temporary one can only deploy that one service.

terms: Who acts: a user, role or service.
A document listing allowed (or denied) actions on resources.
A set of permissions that can be assumed temporarily.
Trusting another identity system (like GitHub) to get temporary credentials.
insights: Whoever can change IAM can grant themselves anything. Treat iam:* and iam:PassRole on broad resources as admin rights in review.
Give humans access the same way as workloads: short SSO sessions into roles, not IAM users with long-lived keys.

prod.summary: In production IAM fails in two ways: too broad (a leaked key can do anything) or too narrow in a confusing way (AccessDenied in the middle of a deploy). Seniors remove long-lived keys, use roles with tight trust policies (especially the OIDC sub condition), and find unused permissions with Access Analyzer.
checklist: No long-lived access keys for workloads; EC2/ECS/Lambda use roles, CI uses OIDC federation.
OIDC trust policies pin both aud and sub (repo and branch or environment), never repo:org/*.
Policies list specific actions and resource ARNs; any "Action": "*" needs a written reason.
Root user has MFA, no access keys, and is used only for the few tasks that need it.
IAM Access Analyzer reviewed for public or cross-account access and unused permissions.
CloudTrail on in all regions, logs kept in a separate account.
Explicit denies (SCPs) for dangerous actions: leaving the organisation, disabling CloudTrail, unused regions.
numbers: IAM policy evaluation: an explicit Deny always wins over any Allow; with no Allow, the default is deny.
A customer-managed IAM policy can be at most 6,144 characters (whitespace not counted); a role can have 20 managed policies attached by default, adjustable to 25.
Role trust policies are limited to 2,048 characters by default (adjustable to 8,192).
Role sessions last 1 hour by default; a role's maximum session can be set from 1 to 12 hours; role chaining (using a role to assume another) is limited to 1 hour.
failures: Deploy fails with User: arn:aws:sts::123:assumed-role/deploy/... is not authorized to perform: ecs:UpdateService on resource ....
The role lacks one action on that resource. Add exactly that action on that ARN; read the full message, it names both. Do not jump to AdministratorAccess.
A fork or a different repo in your GitHub org can assume the production deploy role.
The trust policy used StringLike with repo:org/*. Pin token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub to repo:org/app:environment:production or a protected branch.
GitHub Actions fails with “Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity”.
The token's sub does not match the trust condition (often a job using an environment, which changes the sub format), or id-token: write permission is missing in the workflow.
A key committed to a public repo; within minutes, instances appear in unused regions.
Bots scan GitHub for keys. Deactivate the key immediately, check CloudTrail for what it did, delete created resources, then move that workload to roles.
Allow policy looks right, but access is still denied.
An explicit Deny somewhere wins: an SCP, a permission boundary, a bucket policy or a KMS key policy. Use the policy simulator and check all layers.

code.title: Trust policy: only the production environment of one repo may assume the role
code.note: The sub condition is the security boundary. Without it, any GitHub repository could ask for this role. The workflow also needs permissions: id-token: write.

qs.s: A role has an identity policy allowing s3:* on the bucket. The bucket policy has an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteObject to everyone except an admin role. Can the role delete objects?
o: No; the explicit Deny in the bucket policy wins over the Allow
Yes; identity policies override bucket policies
Yes; s3:* includes delete
Only if the bucket is in the same account
qs.e: IAM evaluates all applicable policies. Any explicit Deny ends the evaluation with deny, wherever it lives.

qs.s: Which OIDC trust condition for a GitHub Actions deploy role is safest?
o: StringLike sub = repo:acme/*
StringEquals aud = sts.amazonaws.com only
No condition; the OIDC provider is already trusted
StringEquals aud = sts.amazonaws.com and sub = repo:acme/api:environment:production
qs.e: Without a tight sub, any repo (in the org, or on GitHub at all) can get a token the role accepts. Pinning to an environment also lets GitHub's environment protection rules gate production.

qs.s: A service needs to read objects under reports/ in one bucket. Which policy is right?
o: s3:* on *
s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-data/reports/*
s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-data
AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess managed policy
qs.e: Object actions apply to object ARNs (bucket/prefix/*); the bare bucket ARN matches no objects. The managed policy reads every bucket in the account.

qs.s: A service with this policy can download reports, but ListObjectsV2 on the bucket fails with AccessDenied. Why?

code.title: reports-reader.json

o: s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action, so it must be granted on arn:aws:s3:::acme-data (optionally limited with an s3:prefix condition), not on object ARNs
ListObjectsV2 needs s3:*
The Version date is too old
Listing is only possible for the root user
qs.e: Object actions match object ARNs (bucket/key); bucket actions match the bucket ARN. A policy that grants ListBucket on objects grants nothing. The s3:prefix condition keeps listing limited to reports/.

qs.s: A SaaS monitoring vendor asks you to create a role it can assume from its AWS account. Your draft trust policy is below. What is missing?

code.title: vendor-trust.json

o: A Deny statement for all other accounts
MFA for the vendor's servers
Nothing; trusting the vendor account is enough
A condition on sts:ExternalId with the unique ID the vendor gave you, so another vendor customer cannot trick the vendor into assuming your role (the “confused deputy” problem)
qs.e: The vendor's account assumes roles for all its customers. Without an external ID, an attacker who is also a customer could enter your role ARN in their own settings. The external ID ties the request to your tenant.

qs.s: A deploy fails with this error. The identity policy of the role allows ec2:RunInstances on *. What should you do?

code.title: deploy log
code.src:
An error occurred (UnauthorizedOperation) when calling the RunInstances operation:
You are not authorized to perform this operation. User:
arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/deploy/gha-8812 is not authorized to perform:
ec2:RunInstances on resource: arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:123456789012:instance/*
with an explicit deny in a service control policy

o: Attach AdministratorAccess to the role
Add a second Allow for RunInstances to the role
Check the region: an SCP denies eu-west-1 (or this action). Deploy to an allowed region, or ask the organisation admins to change the SCP; no change in the account can override it
Recreate the role with a new name
qs.e: AWS now says which policy type caused the deny. An explicit deny in an SCP wins over any Allow in the account, so editing the role cannot help.

qs.s: A Lambda role has s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-docs/*. Reading some objects works, but objects encrypted with a customer managed KMS key fail with AccessDenied. What is needed?
o: s3:GetObjectAcl
Permission to use the key: kms:Decrypt on that key in the role's policy, and a key policy that allows the account (or the role) to use it
Public access on the bucket
Nothing; S3 decrypts SSE-KMS objects for anyone with GetObject
qs.e: With SSE-KMS, S3 calls KMS on your behalf, so the caller needs both the S3 permission and KMS permission. KMS key policies are a separate lock: if the key policy does not allow it, IAM policies alone are not enough.

interview.q: How would you give a CI/CD pipeline access to AWS without storing keys?
answer: Use OIDC federation: register the CI's OIDC provider (e.g. token.actions.githubusercontent.com) in IAM.
Create a deploy role whose trust policy checks aud = sts.amazonaws.com and pins sub to one repo and a protected branch or environment (repo:org/app:environment:production).
Give the role only what deploys need: push to one ECR repo, update one ECS service, pass one task role.
Separate roles per environment and per account; production gated by environment approvals.
Credentials last about an hour, so nothing long-lived exists to leak; CloudTrail shows each session.
followups: What goes wrong if sub uses StringLike repo:org/*?
How would you let the pipeline deploy to several accounts?

interview.q: Explain how AWS decides whether a request is allowed.
answer: Default deny; any explicit Deny in any applicable policy ends it with deny.
Organisation SCPs (and RCPs) set the maximum for member accounts; permission boundaries and session policies further cap a principal.
Within those caps, an Allow is needed from an identity policy or a resource policy (bucket, KMS key, queue).
Cross-account access needs both sides: the caller's identity policy and the resource's policy (or a role trust).
Some services add their own lock, like KMS key policies.
Debug with the full error text (it names the policy type), the policy simulator and CloudTrail.
followups: Can a bucket policy alone grant access to a role in the same account?
What does a permissions boundary not do?

interview.q: How do you get to least privilege in practice without blocking every team?
answer: Start from managed baselines per role type, then narrow with evidence: IAM Access Analyzer can generate policies from CloudTrail activity and flags unused permissions.
Guardrails centrally (SCPs, permission boundaries), freedom inside them, so teams can create roles safely.
Policies written in IaC, reviewed in PRs, with linting (Access Analyzer policy validation) in CI.
Short-lived access for humans through SSO; break-glass roles with alerts for rare admin needs.
Review regularly: remove unused roles, keys and permissions.
followups: How do you handle a team that needs a new permission urgently?
How would you find unused permissions?

diagrams.title: GitHub Actions gets AWS credentials with OIDC
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant GH as GitHub Actions job
  participant O as GitHub OIDC
  participant STS as AWS STS
  participant ECS as ECS service
  GH->>O: request ID token (id-token write)
  O-->>GH: signed JWT, sub = repo:acme/api:environment:production

one: Automatically adding or removing instances based on load metrics.
an: A supermarket opening more checkouts when queues grow and closing them when it is quiet.
how: Horizontal autoscaling adds instances (Kubernetes HPA, cloud autoscaling groups) based on CPU, memory, request rate, or queue depth.
Scaling has lag: metrics are averaged, then new instances boot and warm up. Sudden spikes outrun it; keep headroom or scale on leading signals.
Scale workers on queue depth, not CPU, since a backlog is the real signal.
why: Pay for capacity you need, survive daily peaks, and handle growth without manual work.
trade: Scaling the app tier does nothing if the database is the bottleneck; it can make it worse by adding connections. Set max limits so a bug or attack cannot scale you into a giant bill.

myth.m: With autoscaling we can handle any traffic.
myth.r: You scale until the shared bottleneck (DB, third-party rate limit, budget cap) says no.

q.s: During a sale, autoscaling adds 40 app instances and the site gets slower. Most likely reason?
o: Too few instances
The database is the bottleneck, and more instances add more connections and contention
DNS
CDN
q.e: Find the real bottleneck. Scaling stateless tiers only helps if the stateful tier keeps up.

more: Scaling on custom metrics (queue depth, requests per target)
KEDA for event-driven scaling in Kubernetes
Predictive / scheduled scaling for known peaks
lab: On kind, deploy a CPU-heavy app with a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (target 50% CPU). Generate load and watch kubectl get hpa -w.
Stop the load and watch it scale back down after the stabilisation window.

plain:
Autoscaling adds more copies of your app when load is high and removes them when it is low, based on a metric like CPU usage or queue length.

It is not instant: metrics are measured over time and new instances need time to start. And it only helps the part being scaled; if the database is the bottleneck, more app copies make things worse.
bridge: Serverless platforms do this automatically per request. With containers or VMs, you configure the rules yourself.

walk.title: A sale goes badly, then well
steps: Rule: keep average CPU around 60%; between 2 and 20 instances.
The sale starts. CPU rises to 90%. After about a minute, the autoscaler adds instances; each needs 40 seconds to start.
Instances reach 15, but responses get slower. Monitoring shows the database at 100% CPU, not the app.
More app instances meant more database connections and more queries. The bottleneck was never the app.
Next time: optimise the slow queries and add caching first, and add a read replica. Then autoscaling the app actually helps.

terms: The value the autoscaler tries to maintain, like 60% CPU.
Waiting time between scaling actions to avoid flapping.
insights: Pick a metric that rises before users suffer. CPU works for CPU-bound APIs; for I/O-bound services, in-flight requests or latency is a better signal.
Min and max answer different questions: min pays for safety (zone loss, cold caches), max caps the blast radius of a bug and the bill.

prod.summary: In production autoscaling is a control loop with delays: metrics lag, new instances need time to start and warm up, and scale-down can cut off work in progress. Seniors pick a metric that tracks real load, set min/max deliberately, tune scale-down to avoid flapping, and make sure the database and quotas can take the maximum.
checklist: Every pod has CPU/memory requests set; HPA cannot compute utilisation without them.
Min replicas cover a normal peak plus one failed zone; max replicas are capped by what the database and budget can take.
Workers scale on queue depth or age of oldest message (KEDA, or a custom metric), not CPU.
Readiness probes only pass after warm-up, so new instances do not receive traffic too early.
Graceful shutdown handles SIGTERM: stop taking new work, finish in-flight requests within the grace period.
Scheduled scale-up before known peaks (launches, sales, 9 a.m. Monday).
A load test confirms the system at max replicas, not only at min.
numbers: Kubernetes HPA checks metrics every 15 s by default (--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period).

HPA ignores changes within a 10% tolerance by default (--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-tolerance = 0.1); A per-HPA tolerance field (behavior.scaleUp.tolerance / scaleDown.tolerance) was alpha in Kubernetes 1.33, beta and on by default in 1.35, and is GA in 1.37 (feature gate HPAConfigurableTolerance).

Default HPA behavior: scale-down uses a 300 s stabilisation window and may then remove up to 100% of pods per 15 s (down to minReplicas); scale-up has no window and may add the larger of 100% or 4 pods per 15 s.
HPA formula: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric).
failures: kubectl get hpa shows <unknown>/60% and replicas never change.
metrics-server is missing, or pods have no CPU requests. Install metrics-server and set resources.requests.cpu on every container.
Replicas jump 4 → 12 → 4 → 12 every few minutes (flapping).
Scale-down is too eager or the metric is noisy. Keep a scale-down stabilisation window, and limit how many pods can be removed per minute in behavior.
During a spike, new pods start, get traffic, and return 502s for their first 30 s.
Readiness passes before the app is warm (JIT, caches, connection pools). Make readiness depend on real warm-up and use slow-start on the load balancer.
After scaling to 40 pods, Postgres shows too many clients already.
Max replicas × pool size exceeded max_connections. Put a pooler in front and set max replicas from the DB's real capacity.
Users see failed requests every time the cluster scales down.
Pods are killed mid-request. Handle SIGTERM, add a short preStop delay so the load balancer stops routing first, and set a PodDisruptionBudget.

code.title: HPA with fast scale-up and calm scale-down
code.src:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  minReplicas: 3          # one per zone, survives a zone loss
  maxReplicas: 20         # capped by what Postgres can take
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60   # % of the pod's CPU *request*
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      selectPolicy: Max
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100      # may double every 15 s...
          periodSeconds: 15
        - type: Pods
          value: 4        # ...or add 4 pods, whichever is more
          periodSeconds: 15
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 2        # remove at most 2 pods per minute
          periodSeconds: 60
code.note: Utilisation is measured against the CPU request, so the HPA does nothing if requests are missing. The scale-up block spells out the Kubernetes default (fast); the scale-down block is slower than the default, which could drop to minReplicas within seconds once the 300 s window passes.

qs.s: An HPA targets 50% CPU. There are 4 pods averaging 90% CPU. How many replicas will it ask for?
qs.e: ceil(4 × 90 / 50) = ceil(7.2) = 8. The HPA scales in proportion to how far the metric is from the target.

qs.s: Workers process jobs from a queue. Each job mostly waits on an external API, so CPU stays at 15% while the backlog grows to 50,000 jobs. The HPA targets 70% CPU. What is wrong and what fixes it?
o: CPU is the wrong signal for I/O-bound work; scale on queue length or oldest-message age (e.g. with KEDA)
The CPU target is too high; set it to 10%
Add more memory to each worker
Nothing; the backlog will clear at night
qs.e: I/O-bound workers never get busy on CPU, so a CPU-based HPA never scales them. Backlog is the real load signal.

qs.s: You expect a product launch at 10:00 with traffic 8× higher within 2 minutes. New pods need 90 s to become ready. What is the most reliable plan?
o: Trust the HPA; it reacts within 15 s
Lower the CPU target to 20% permanently
Scale up ahead of time (raise minReplicas before 10:00, check DB and quotas), then let the HPA handle the rest and lower min afterwards
Turn off autoscaling during the launch
qs.e: Reactive scaling lags: metrics, then decisions, then 90 s of startup, while the spike arrives in 2 minutes. For known peaks, pre-scale.

qs.s: A Node.js API scales on this HPA. After a traffic spike it grows to 12 pods and never scales back down, though traffic returned to normal hours ago. Why?

code.title: hpa.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70

o: The HPA needs a restart after every spike
Garbage-collected runtimes keep heap they grew and rarely return it to the OS, so memory stays high when load drops; scale on CPU or requests per second, and use memory only as a safety limit
maxReplicas is too high
Memory metrics are only read once per hour
qs.e: Memory often does not follow load in Node, the JVM or Go: it rises with traffic and stays. A metric that does not fall when load falls cannot drive scale-down.

qs.s: An HPA targets 60% CPU. There are 10 pods averaging 64% CPU. With default settings, how many replicas does it ask for?
o: 10 (no change)
qs.e: The ratio is 64 / 60 ≈ 1.067, within the default 10% tolerance, so the HPA does nothing. Without the tolerance it would be ceil(10 × 1.067) = 11. The tolerance stops constant small changes from noisy metrics.

qs.s: During a spike the HPA raised the Deployment to 30 replicas, but the service is still overloaded. What does this output tell you?

o: The HPA only creates pods; the cluster has no room for them. You need node autoscaling (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) with enough headroom and quota, or spare capacity
The pods' readiness probes are too strict
The HPA is broken and should be deleted
The CPU target should be lowered to 20%
qs.e: Pod autoscaling and node autoscaling are separate loops. Pending pods with “Insufficient cpu” mean the nodes are full. Node scaling adds minutes (new VMs), which is another reason to keep headroom for spikes.

qs.s: A spike ends at 10:00 and CPU drops far below the target. The HPA uses default behavior. When does it start removing pods?
o: At about 10:00:15, at the next sync
Never; HPAs only scale up
After about 5 minutes: the 300 s scale-down window uses the highest recommendation of the last 5 minutes. After that, the default policy can remove up to 100% of pods per 15 s, down to minReplicas
After 1 hour, the default cooldown
qs.e: The scale-down stabilisation window prevents flapping by waiting until lower recommendations have held for 300 s. Note the default scale-down after that is fast; add a Pods or Percent policy if you want it gradual.

interview.q: How would you set up autoscaling for an HTTP API and for queue workers?
answer: API: HPA on CPU (with CPU requests set) or on requests per second per pod via a custom metric; target around 50–70% to leave headroom for the scaling delay.
Workers: scale on queue depth or the age of the oldest message (KEDA or a custom metric); CPU says nothing for I/O-bound work.
minReplicas covers normal peak plus a zone loss; maxReplicas comes from what the database, downstream rate limits and budget can take.
Behavior: fast scale-up, calm scale-down (stabilisation window plus a Pods/Percent policy).
Node autoscaling (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) so new pods have somewhere to run; readiness probes and graceful shutdown so scaling does not cause errors.

interview.q: Tell me how autoscaling can make an incident worse.
answer: Scaling the app tier multiplies database connections and queries; if the DB is the bottleneck, latency rises further (more pods → too many clients already).
Retry storms: slow responses cause retries, retries look like load, more pods add more retries to a struggling dependency.
Flapping: noisy metrics plus eager scale-down kill pods mid-request and cold pods take traffic before they are warm.
Cost runaway: a bug or attack scales to max; without a sane maxReplicas and budget alerts, the bill grows.
Mitigations: max limits from real capacity, poolers, circuit breakers and retry budgets, readiness tied to warm-up, scale on the right signal.
followups: How would you load test autoscaling?
What would you alert on?

interview.q: A big launch is next Tuesday at 10:00. How do you prepare the scaling?
answer: Estimate peak traffic and convert it to replicas, connections and node counts using numbers from a load test.
Pre-scale before the event: raise minReplicas (or a scheduled scale action), warm nodes, check service quotas and DB capacity.
Load-test at the planned max, including the database, caches and third-party limits.
Prepare protection: rate limits, a queue for non-urgent work, feature flags to switch off heavy features.
Watch dashboards live, then lower minReplicas afterwards so the bill returns to normal.
